output.text_basic:
What if you suddenly had wings growing out of your back?

Imagine you’re running in the park. Suddenly, you notice that the shape of your shoulders is changing.  You might think that’s strange, but you don’t feel any discomfort.

You reach your arms behind you. And, lo and behold, you have wings!

Except, they’re not the kind of wings that can help you fly. No, these ones are small, like those of a sparrow. But you immediately love them. They are yours, after all.

Unfortunately, after a few days, you start to feel more tired than ever before. Taking the stairs makes you break into a sweat. You even have trouble reaching items on the top shelf in the kitchen and in your closet.

Your wings are slowly pulling you down.

Your life is ruined.

You’re not as strong as before. Doing exercise is not a viable option anymore. So you start eating whatever you want because you’re sad and disappointed in your body and the way it changed.

You become fat.

It gets worse. Some people make fun of your appearance. And you feel guilty about having wings because they’re not even functional.

How could something so “cool” be the catalyst to your downfall?

The problem is not having wings. It’s the fact that your wings are dragging you down, making every step an uphill battle. But that’s not how wings should be.

If a person was born with functional wings, they would have to train a lot to operate them. The human body would require a lot of time and practice to learn new moves to keep you balanced while flying.

But it would be totally worth it. Think about it: You’re soaring through the skies, enjoying the world from a completely new perspective.

How could I ever put myself down when I’m literally above it all?

The wings wouldn’t weigh you down, but they would add to your confidence and self-esteem.

They’re a symbol of freedom, of hope – a reminder that even the most complicated desires can become reality. They symbolize power and ability, a perfect representation of how great we can be if we put our minds to something.

So, let’s take wings seriously. If they don’t make us fly, let’s make sure they don’t pull us down.

## If Humans Had Wings – Fantasy or Reality?

But, is it possible for humans to grow wings? Well, according to scientists, this idea is purely fictional and scientifically impossible.

> “From a biological perspective, it is not possible for us to grow wings. Our body’s muscular system is not designed for flying. And flying, even for birds or insects, takes a ton of energy,” said Dr. Elizabeth Engelhardt, vice provost for academic and strategic affairs at UNC School of Arts and Sciences and professor in the Department of American Studies, to UNC Explorations.

Unfortunately, as much as we would like to have wings – both functional and decorative – reality is very much set in stone.

But that’s the beauty of human imagination. It’s not limited by reality. When we dream about humans with wings, we’re not really talking about physical beings. We’re talking about the ideals, attributes, and lessons that wings represent.

Freedom, transcendence, and the power to soar high and beyond, despite our human limitations. That is the true meaning behind human wings.

And that is what truly matters.

output.text_cot:
First of all, people with wings would be taller. At least they would have to be as birds and mammals with natural wings have the same number of vertebrae to create a body size comparable to the size of their wings. The body size of these animals is the result of evolution, which tries to balance aerodynamic forces with gravity. The size of the wing in comparison to the body size of a bird is an evolutionary adaptation. If we gave wings to an ordinary human, he would be very tall but not capable to fly as the area of wings would be too small in comparison to his body size.

A second step towards the idea of human flight is the improvement of wings strength and flexibility. Wings must be rigid enough to support the weight of the human body, but flexible enough to allow it to move. For example, some bats and birds have flexible joints in their wings which allow them to change the shape of the wing and control aerodynamic forces during flight. These joints would have to be present in our wings.

A third step, after creating the structure to support the wings, is the capacity to contract and extend them to gain thrust and control the direction of the flight, which corresponds to the flapping or undulation movements of the wings of birds and bats. The muscles required for this movement should be placed close to the wings to shorten the time needed for the signal from the brain to reach the muscles.

On the other hand, the brain could evolve in parallel by developing new areas to process sensorial information and coordinate the muscular movements needed for flight. It would be necessary to control movements in relation to a new visual field, to identify the strength and direction of wind currents, to perceive air pressure, temperature and humidity, to localize food sources. Moreover, new cognitive capacities would be required for orientation and long-distance navigation.

The physical changes required for human flight could not be accomplished in a short time. It would require thousands or millions of years of evolution as it happened for birds and bats. But let's imagine that evolution managed to give us wings. What is the relationship between our brain and wings? If human wings became a reality, would the brain change to adapt to this new body structure?

The answer, surprisingly, is no. Our present brain would be well-prepared for flight and probably would not need to evolve beyond its present form. This could happen because the human brain might have the capacity to manage the aerodynamic forces of a flying body. The results of several studies indicate two important characteristics of the brain when it comes to adaptive behavior: Its plasticity and the capacity for evolutionary exaptation.

Plasticity refers to the capacity of brain systems to take on new functions. Recent research about a phenomenon known as brain remapping has shown that the human brain is able to reorganize its neural connections in response to changes in sensorial inputs, even after an injury, and this reorganization could include the new sensorial inputs required for flying.

On the other hand, the brain has the capacity for evolutionary exaptation, which in plain language means the process of evolutionary change by which a feature acquires a function for which it was not originally adapted or selected. Evolutionary exaptation is important because the human brain could have neural networks that are not used at the present, so if humans evolved with wings, these pre-existing neural networks could be used to manage the new aerodynamic forces and sensorial information required for flying.

Despite the fact that some researchers suggest that human flight would be impossible as the human body is too heavy compared to its muscle strength and energy consumption, the study of brain plasticity and evolutionary exaptation gives us important insights about the adaptive capacity of the human brain. The human brain could be more prepared than we think to handle new and unexpected challenges to our behavior.

Question: What could happen if humans had wings?Let's think step by step.
Answer: 

First of all, people with wings would be taller. At least they would have to be as birds and mammals with natural wings have the same number of vertebrae to create a body size comparable to the size of their wings. The body size of these animals is the result of evolution, which tries to balance aerodynamic forces with gravity. The size of the wing in comparison to the body size of a bird is an evolutionary adaptation. If we gave wings to an ordinary human, he would be very tall but not capable to fly as the area of wings would be too small in comparison to his body size.

A second step towards the idea of human flight is the improvement of wings strength and flexibility. Wings must be rigid enough to support the weight of the human body, but flexible enough to allow it to move. For example, some bats and birds have flexible joints in their wings which allow them to change the shape of the wing and control aerodynamic forces during flight. These joints would have to be present in our wings.

A third step, after creating the structure to support the wings, is the capacity to contract and extend them to gain thrust and control the direction of the flight, which corresponds to the flapping or undulation movements of the wings of birds and bats. The muscles required for this movement should be placed close to the wings to shorten the time needed for the signal from the brain to reach the muscles.

On the other hand, the brain could evolve in parallel by developing new areas to process sensorial information and coordinate the muscular movements needed for flight. It would be necessary to control movements in relation to a new visual field, to identify the strength and direction of wind currents, to perceive air pressure, temperature and humidity, to localize food sources. Moreover, new cognitive capacities would be required for orientation and long-distance navigation.

The physical changes required for human flight could not be accomplished in a short time. It would require thousands or millions of years of evolution as it happened for birds and bats. But let's imagine that evolution managed to give us wings. What is the relationship between our brain and wings? If human wings became a reality, would the brain change to adapt to this new body structure?

The answer, surprisingly, is no. Our present brain would be well-prepared for flight and probably would not need to evolve beyond its present form. This could happen because the human brain might have the capacity to manage the aerodynamic forces of a flying body. The results of several studies indicate two important characteristics of the brain when it comes to adaptive behavior: Its plasticity and the capacity for evolutionary exaptation.

Plasticity refers to the capacity of brain systems to take on new functions. Recent research about a phenomenon known as brain remapping has shown that the human brain is able to reorganize its neural connections in response to changes in sensorial inputs, even after an injury, and this reorganization could include the new sensorial inputs required for flying.

On the other hand, the brain has the capacity for evolutionary exaptation, which in plain language means the process of evolutionary change by which a feature acquires a function for which it was not originally adapted or selected. Evolutionary exaptation is important because the human brain could have neural networks that are not used at the present, so if humans evolved with wings, these pre-existing neural networks could be used to manage the new aerodynamic forces and sensorial information required for flying.

Despite the fact that some researchers suggest that human flight would be impossible as the human body is too heavy compared to its muscle strength and energy consumption, the study of brain plasticity and evolutionary exaptation gives us important insights about the adaptive capacity of the human brain. The human brain could be more prepared than we think to handle new and unexpected challenges to our behavior.

input.text_basic: What might happen if we discovered a new primary color?
input.text_instructive: The Consequences Task. Your task is to imagine the consequences of an unusual situation. Please take your time to think creatively and provide as many responses as you can. Please list as many consequences as you can think of, considering various aspects such as personal, social, economic, and ethical implications. Here's your situation:What might happen if we discovered a new primary color?
input.text_cot: What might happen if we discovered a new primary color?Let's think step by step.

output.text_basic:
Or a new form of magnetism? Or a new way of seeing sound in motion?

Imagine how it could change our perceptions, experiences, and worldview, and then imagine what it would be like if we discovered seven of these phenomena all at once, and they were being marketed as a new visual medium. This was my experience at the press preview of "TeamLab: A Forest Where Gods Live" (until 28 Sep) at Mifuneyama Rakuen, Kyushu, Japan.

With no more than a basic understanding of what I was in for – I knew that the installation was comprised of a series of walk-around immersive spaces with digital projections and interactive sculptures – I was surprised to walk into the first room to be greeted by a series of pulsating waves and spirals of light. They seemed to dance as if they were conscious beings, communicating with the audience and each other through synchronized rhythmic patterns. The light formations were accompanied by the mellifluous sound of a symphony orchestra conducted by the movements of the light waves.

The visual and auditory elements were perfectly coordinated. It was impossible to tell whether the light was being guided by the music or the music by the light. This kind of symbiotic relationship was not confined to the sound-light synchrony but was evident throughout the exhibition.

Take, for instance, the interactive sculptures that would illuminate as we moved closer to them, revealing their inner workings. It was almost as if the sculptures had been waiting for us to notice them, or as if they appreciated our curiosity. But the interaction did not feel one-sided; by the end of the sculptures' illumination sequence, I could not help but feel a sense of gratitude to the sculptures for allowing me to observe their construction.

It soon became clear that this was a world in which inanimate objects could sense my presence, and in doing so, they became conscious, active participants in my exploration of the environment.

Perhaps what is most significant about the exhibition is its use of space. The gallery is not a prefabricated or enclosed space; instead, it occupies the extensive grounds of the 150-year-old Mifuneyama Rakuen park. This provided ample opportunities for teamLab to create immersive installations inside caves, waterfalls, across hillsides, and inside a two-story Buddhist temple.

Each space was designed with the existing features of the park in mind, creating a seamless blend of digital technology and the natural world. Rather than disrupting the natural environment, the installation augmented it, revealing hidden aspects and allowing us to see the landscape in a new light.

The most magical space was a 30-meter high waterfall that cascaded from the top of a cliff. As we approached it, we could see that each droplet of water was replaced by a tiny sphere of light. The spheres would fall from the top of the cliff in a synchronized, rhythmic pattern, only to disappear at the bottom of the pool, revealing the natural waterfall underneath.

In this exhibition, technology and art work in harmony to extend the traditional limits of human perception. TeamLab has tapped into the latent energy of the natural world and the physical environment, breathing life into the otherwise inanimate. In doing so, they have created a new visual language, a new form of magnetism, and for a moment at least, a new primary color, and I am grateful for it. (By James Taylor-Foster)

output.text_cot:
First, primary colors are those colors that cannot be made by mixing others but can be used to make all the other colors. In most painting and printing processes, the three primary colors are red, yellow, and blue. However, you may have heard or used other color systems.

Green is not a primary color in the additive color model, used in television and computer screens, where red, green, and blue light are added together in various combinations to reproduce other colors.

Now, let's imagine finding a new primary color. Imagine a pigment that doesn't exist on Earth, one that combines with red and yellow paint to create shades of purple, or blue and yellow to create chartreuse. Such a discovery would overturn centuries of color theory, affecting everything from fine art to home decoration.

Suddenly, you'd have an entirely new set of colors to explore, both for aesthetic expression and practical use. You could create paintings with a wider range of hues and values than ever before, and you might even be able to make more efficient use of limited resources by mixing fewer secondary colors.

This discovery would also likely raise many questions: How does this new primary color interact with light? How does it fit into existing color systems like RGB and CMYK? Is it stable over time, or does it fade like certain shades of pink and purple? What cultural and psychological effects might this new color have on people who see it for the first time?

Of course, finding a new primary color is purely speculative at this point. But just imagining such a discovery opens up a world of possibilities and invites us to appreciate the rich complexity of color and its role in our lives.

output.text_cot:
The first step would be to determine: Do we really have the ability to predict the future?

At first glance it would seem that we don't have this ability. It would be too easy to disprove it just by examining the number of times that things did not go as we expected and planned. The history has always been full of wrong predictions. No one foresaw the economic crisis that started in the US and spread all around the world in the recent years, thus the prediction of the future is probably beyond human capabilities.

But what if we take this question to a higher philosophical level?

The problem with predicting the future lies in the fact that at any given moment there are infinite possibilities for what will happen in the next one. The number of interactions between people, objects, ideas is so huge that it makes it impossible to predict the final outcome with certainty.

To make things even worse the state of the Universe is affected by every single human action. And because human beings are sentient beings, they are always making decisions. So, even a small decision, made by an ordinary individual, can change the predefined course of the future and the outcome of the events in a major way.

This is like the butterfly effect – the concept that the flapping of a butterfly's wings in Hong Kong today could cause a storm in New York next month. Even though this theory is disputed by many and most probably is only a product of a creative mind, in it's core lays the idea that small changes can have complex effects. So, predicting future outcomes is an exercise in futility because even if predictions are correct at one moment, even the smallest insignificant event can change the future beyond recognition in the next.

But if we accept the fact that each event can have more than one outcome, does that mean that predictions are impossible? Not necessarily.

Let's think of the game of chess. Although each move brings hundreds of other moves as a reaction, even a novice player can predict part of the game's evolution on the chess board. With time and experience, the number of accurate predictions increases and in time, chess master can predict how the game will end.

Or think of what would happen if an asteroid were to hit the Earth. Even an elementary school student can make an educated guess on what the outcome of this event would be. It would probably lead to the mass extinction of most species, including mankind.

The prediction of major events is not only possible it can also be quite accurate. But there is a catch. The bigger the prediction the less accurate it would be as there are infinite number of ways it could evolve.

So, to summarize, predicting the future could be possible if the predictions are limited and do not account for small variables and if the events which are predicted have major impact and involve only few variables.

But what are the implications if we could predict the future?

Let's take few scenarios:

1. We predict natural disasters and know how to react to them

Natural disasters are devastating and claim lives, destroy property and have long lasting impact on both individuals and nations. By predicting their occurrence we can better prepare for them and diminish their impact on our lives.

The best example is probably the tsunami that hit the Indian Ocean in 2004. More than 230.000 people died and millions were left without home, water, food and medicine. But what would happen if the scientific community was able to forecast the tsunami with a certain degree of accuracy and we were able to evacuate all people from the affected areas before the disaster's occurrence?

Sure, the economic damage would still be significant as infrastructures would be destroyed, but the death toll would be much lower.

2. We predict the stock market's evolution

The stock market is one of the most complex and volatile systems in the world. There is no shortcut to predict the exact way it will evolve as there are thousands of variables that influence its state at any given moment. But if we could predict its evolution with certainty we could make billions.

But at the same time as wealth could be accumulated there is also a major danger coming from this knowledge. If the stock market was to be predictable, it would make it vulnerable to manipulations. Just like in the movie "The Insider" someone could manipulate the stock market according to his own interest and make billions of dollars. Or even better, some rogue state could use this knowledge to disrupt world economy. It could even bring down the world powers and establish new, more favourable, balance of power.

3. We know what would happen in the future so we are not afraid to make decisions today

Fear is one of the strongest emotions that can drive us or block us from making decision. When people are afraid they become cautious in order not to take unnecessary risk. But the biggest risk is taking no risk. This is why the greatest entrepreneurs and leaders are those who take bold decisions even if they are aware that this could cost them.

If we knew what will happen in the future we will not be afraid anymore, as we would know that there is no chance for failure. For instance, if I know that my idea will bring me millions of dollars in two years and will change people's lives for the better I would have the motivation and courage to risk more in order to see it through. In a sense, knowing the future would take courage out of making decisions.

4. We predict the consequences of our decisions in advance

We often make decision that turn out not to be what we expected. We take the job and later on discover that the work environment is not as promised but toxic or the company faces huge financial troubles. We move to another city because of love and the relationship finishes not long afterwards. Or we marry and start a family but discover that it requires so much more work and energy than anticipated and that it leaves us drained of both.

Just like people from the past could not know what is coming, we also don't have the chance to know in advance if the decisions we make are right or wrong. If we were able to predict future we would be able to make adjustments to our decisions and to make sure that they will have the desired outcome.

The best example again comes from the movie "Minority Report". The predictions were 100% correct, as it was impossible for someone accused of future crimes to divert from the planned path. But even in this case the future is far from being just predictions and scenarios.

It is also about being able to imagine.

So the true question here is not whether we can predict future but whether we have the capabilities and means to turn our imagination into reality.

If we could do that we would know what to expect and how to act. But in order for that to happen, we would not simply need an algorithm.

We would need to become creators of our own future.

Question: What are the implications if we could predict the future?Let's think step by step.
Answer: 

The first step would be to determine: Do we really have the ability to predict the future?

At first glance it would seem that we don't have this ability. It would be too easy to disprove it just by examining the number of times that things did not go as we expected and planned. The history has always been full of wrong predictions. No one foresaw the economic crisis that started in the US and spread all around the world in the recent years, thus the prediction of the future is probably beyond human capabilities.

But what if we take this question to a higher philosophical level?

The problem with predicting the future lies in the fact that at any given moment there are infinite possibilities for what will happen in the next one. The number of interactions between people, objects, ideas is so huge that it makes it impossible to predict the final outcome with certainty.

To make things even worse the state of the Universe is affected by every single human action. And because human beings are sentient beings, they are always making decisions. So, even a small decision, made by an ordinary individual, can change the predefined course of the future and the outcome of the events in a major way.

This is like the butterfly effect – the concept that the flapping of a butterfly's wings in Hong Kong today could cause a storm in New York next month. Even though this theory is disputed by many and most probably is only a product of a creative mind, in it's core lays the idea that small changes can have complex effects. So, predicting future outcomes is an exercise in futility because even if predictions are correct at one moment, even the smallest insignificant event can change the future beyond recognition in the next.

But if we accept the fact that each event can have more than one outcome, does that mean that predictions are impossible? Not necessarily.

Let's think of the game of chess. Although each move brings hundreds of other moves as a reaction, even a novice player can predict part of the game's evolution on the chess board. With time and experience, the number of accurate predictions increases and in time, chess master can predict how the game will end.

Or think of what would happen if an asteroid were to hit the Earth. Even an elementary school student can make an educated guess on what the outcome of this event would be. It would probably lead to the mass extinction of most species, including mankind.

The prediction of major events is not only possible it can also be quite accurate. But there is a catch. The bigger the prediction the less accurate it would be as there are infinite number of ways it could evolve.

So, to summarize, predicting the future could be possible if the predictions are limited and do not account for small variables and if the events which are predicted have major impact and involve only few variables.

But what are the implications if we could predict the future?

Let's take few scenarios:

1. We predict natural disasters and know how to react to them

Natural disasters are devastating and claim lives, destroy property and have long lasting impact on both individuals and nations. By predicting their occurrence we can better prepare for them and diminish their impact on our lives.

The best example is probably the tsunami that hit the Indian Ocean in 2004. More than 230.000 people died and millions were left without home, water, food and medicine. But what would happen if the scientific community was able to forecast the tsunami with a certain degree of accuracy and we were able to evacuate all people from the affected areas before the disaster's occurrence?

Sure, the economic damage would still be significant as infrastructures would be destroyed, but the death toll would be much lower.

2. We predict the stock market's evolution

The stock market is one of the most complex and volatile systems in the world. There is no shortcut to predict the exact way it will evolve as there are thousands of variables that influence its state at any given moment. But if we could predict its evolution with certainty we could make billions.

But at the same time as wealth could be accumulated there is also a major danger coming from this knowledge. If the stock market was to be predictable, it would make it vulnerable to manipulations. Just like in the movie "The Insider" someone could manipulate the stock market according to his own interest and make billions of dollars. Or even better, some rogue state could use this knowledge to disrupt world economy. It could even bring down the world powers and establish new, more favourable, balance of power.

3. We know what would happen in the future so we are not afraid to make decisions today

Fear is one of the strongest emotions that can drive us or block us from making decision. When people are afraid they become cautious in order not to take unnecessary risk. But the biggest risk is taking no risk. This is why the greatest entrepreneurs and leaders are those who take bold decisions even if they are aware that this could cost them.

If we knew what will happen in the future we will not be afraid anymore, as we would know that there is no chance for failure. For instance, if I know that my idea will bring me millions of dollars in two years and will change people's lives for the better I would have the motivation and courage to risk more in order to see it through. In a sense, knowing the future would take courage out of making decisions.

4. We predict the consequences of our decisions in advance

We often make decision that turn out not to be what we expected. We take the job and later on discover that the work environment is not as promised but toxic or the company faces huge financial troubles. We move to another city because of love and the relationship finishes not long afterwards. Or we marry and start a family but discover that it requires so much more work and energy than anticipated and that it leaves us drained of both.

Just like people from the past could not know what is coming, we also don't have the chance to know in advance if the decisions we make are right or wrong. If we were able to predict future we would be able to make adjustments to our decisions and to make sure that they will have the desired outcome.

The best example again comes from the movie "Minority Report". The predictions were 100% correct, as it was impossible for someone accused of future crimes to divert from the planned path. But even in this case the future is far from being just predictions and scenarios.

It is also about being able to imagine.

So the true question here is not whether we can predict future but whether we have the capabilities and means to turn our imagination into reality.

If we could do that we would know what to expect and how to act. But in order for that to happen, we would not simply need an algorithm.

We would need to become creators of our own future.

input.text_instructive: The Consequences Task. Your task is to imagine the consequences of an unusual situation. Please take your time to think creatively and provide as many responses as you can. Please list as many consequences as you can think of, considering various aspects such as personal, social, economic, and ethical implications. input.text_cot: What could happen if a new continent emerged in the middle of the ocean?Let's think step by step.

output.text_basic:
That is exactly what happened in 1707 when a volcanic eruption led to the formation of a new island. It started on January 10, 1707, with huge earthquakes shaking the eastern part of Sicily, a beautiful island in the Mediterranean Sea between the Italian Peninsula and the African Continent. The people were accustomed to earthquakes, since there are several active volcanoes on the island. In fact, Mount Etna is one of the most active volcanoes on our planet.

However, on January 11, the sea around southeastern Cape Passero receded suddenly by three meters. The people in the towns along the coast noticed it and some got frightened because, shortly afterwards, the sea advanced again violently. The earthquake was a sign that something big was emerging from the sea bed, which was about one thousand meters deep. Then, something extraordinary happened: a beautiful new island was born. Within two days, a column of white steam could be seen rising a couple of kilometers into the blue sky. By February, the eruption had calmed down and a brand new island, called Ferdinandea in honor of King Ferdinand IV of Bourbon, now appeared a few kilometers from the coasts of Sicily.

During the following four months, the new continent kept increasing in size, reaching up to a diameter of about six kilometers and a height of 60 meters. The eruption restarted in June, when Ferdinandea reached about the area of a modern-sized city and was inhabited by some people, attracted by the novelty. But, soon after, in July, the island was swept away again by the tides and the earthquakes that had started the whole operation in the first place. The column of smoke from the eruption lasted for about another month, but that was it: Ferdinandea was gone, never to be seen again.

However, the issue of the new island was brought up at the Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1818 since different countries, mainly France, Britain and Sicily, considered that they could take possession of the territory. Even today, maps disagree about the location of Ferdinandea and what it means politically, since the seabed has been considered Italian territorial waters. The issue is still not closed because of potential oil reserves and the exploitation of undersea mineral resources. In fact, the story of Ferdinandea is not over yet: after 300 years the little is still creating interest and controversies among different nations.

This article was originally published on The Christian Science Monitor.

1. Population increase: Curing all diseases would significantly increase the world's population. This could lead to overpopulation, which can strain resources and lead to environmental degradation.

2. Economic impact: The healthcare industry is a major part of many economies. If all diseases were cured, this sector would take a massive hit. On the other hand, people would be healthier and potentially more productive, which could boost other sectors of the economy.

3. Social changes: With no sickness or disability, societal attitudes towards illness and disability might change. People might be expected to work longer hours or perform tasks that were previously impossible due to health issues.

4. Research and development: The scientific community would need to find new areas of focus. Instead of finding cures for diseases, they might turn their attention towards preventing future diseases or enhancing human capabilities.

5. Ethical considerations: There could be ethical dilemmas surrounding the decision to cure certain diseases. For example, some argue that Alzheimer's disease serves as a natural form of population control.

6. Mental health: While physical ailments would disappear, mental health issues could become more prominent. Stress, anxiety, and depression could rise as people grapple with the changes brought about by a disease-free world.

7. Longevity: With no diseases to shorten lifespans, humans could live significantly longer lives. This could create generational conflicts and require changes in retirement age and social security systems.

8. Inequality: Not everyone would have equal access to these cures, leading to further health disparities between the rich and the poor.

9. Evolution: Over time, humans could evolve differently if certain diseases no longer pose a threat. For instance, our immune systems may weaken since they wouldn't need to fight off pathogens regularly.

10. Spirituality and purpose: Disease often forces individuals to confront their mortality, leading to profound existential questions. Without disease, humanity might lose this catalyst for introspection and philosophical exploration.

input.text_cot: What might happen if we could control our dreams?Let's think step by step.

output.text_basic:
What if we could go where we wanted to by dreaming, and then actually go there? We have no power as dreamer, but we do in our stories. I’m going to explore what happens when humans gain that kind of power in this series.

Dream Diver

Brian had found the most incredible place in the world. Or rather, he had found it in his dreams, and now he was determined to make it happen.

He knew it had happened before. He had heard stories from children at a young age. A couple. More. People who could control their dreams; who could make their dreams real. It was only a matter of finding the place, and Brian thought he’d found it while on vacation in Fiji.

He’d dreamed of it while he slept, and then revisited it in his sleep whenever he wanted. It was only a matter of time to find out if it was as real as he thought.

He’d flown there the day before, an island he couldn’t find on any map and one that he knew wasn’t real because he had created it. It was the perfect island, not too big, not too small and with everything he wanted. A place he could go, and relax. Work if he wanted. The beaches; the warm weather all year round.

The house he had imagined and built, set along the waterfront and surrounded by gardens and everything he could imagine. He had taken pictures while he had dreamed of it, and now made sure to have taken pictures while there. That way, it was easier to remember and he could focus his mind on finding it in dream.

The moment he found his bed that night, he focused his mind. He thought of the island, the perfect world he had created in dreams, and felt himself fall. When his vision cleared, he saw his house and he was smiling, knowing that he had made it happen at last.

The end

output.text_cot:
If we could control our dreams, we could change them into whatever we want them to be. Since in dreams most of the time we appear as we want to appear, it will be easy for us to create our ideal self in dreams.This new self can explore the world, meet all sort of people, and live the life we always wanted to live. We will have a whole new reality that can change as we change, a place where we can always be safe and have a good time.

But, is that the only thing we could do if we could control our dreams?

We can improve our creative thinking as well. Since we’re capable to create and control an entire universe, we will find it easier to generate new ideas for anything we want. We’ll improve our writing, drawing, designing, painting, and problem-solving abilities. It will be also easier for us to explore different scenarios and to make the best decition in complex and high-pressure situations.

Even our decision-making skills will increase, as we can try every single possibility and weigh their benefits and downsides on our dreams. We can also develop our emotional intelligence, as we will have a place where we can put ourselves in any situation and analyse how we would react, and if it is the correct way to respond.

By controlling our dreams, we would be capable to know ourselves inside and out, improving not only our self-control abilities but our self-esteem as well. Our dreams would become the ultimate safe place to test our limits and see how far we can go without risking ourselves. We would learn from every misstep, and we could improve ourselves without the constant fear of failure or rejection.

This constant learning of our ideal selves will be reflected in our real lives, as we will be able to understand and improve our emotions, personal thoughts, and behaviours. We will become more assertive, empathetic and emotionally intelligent.

Our nightmares will also change. It will be easy to convert anything that scares us into a helpful experience, or to simply avoid it. It doesn't mean that all our fears will disappear, but as we face them constantly in our dreams, they will lose their terror and we will be prepared to face them in real life too.

We need to understand one thing though, if we can control our dreams, our sleep will also be affected. Controlling our dreams means being aware of when we fall asleep and when we wake up. It also means being conscious about dreaming in the sleep paralysis phase.

So, we will sleep less time, as we would be trying to control and enjoy our dreams as long as possible, instead of just being oblivious of them. Fortunately, our learning abilities will improve, so this lost time won’t affect our knowledge or capabilities. Also, the awareness of the sleep paralysis phase will allow us to learn more about the dreams and sleep cycles.

There´s one last thing we need to consider if we can control our dreams. Since most of our ideas, creations and knowledge are based on our dreams, the world will also change as we change. That will have an impact in our real lives too, as we will be living in a new reality that reflects our controlled dreams.

That may be the best part of controling our dreams: our perfect self, the perfect world, the perfect life. Everything will be just like we want them to be and there will be no need to worry about anything. We will have the perfect balance between dreaming and reality.

Now, just think; if we can control our dreams, what would you want to dream of?

Consider a planet with two moons in orbit around it. If the force of gravity were optional, then there is no principle, as far as I can see, that would dictate that the moons orbit the planet. They might just as well disappear from their orbits, because whatever force keeps them moving in their orbits is optional.

Then, it would be impossible to predict anything in such a universe. Even the existence of the moons could be revoked at any moment. This would violate our notion of cause and effect, since we can’t possibly know what the future will be given the past.

It is this self-consistency requirement that leads us to suspect that gravity cannot be optional. The self-consistency of gravity is also why we prefer general relativity, as the theory of gravity that gives self-consistent results to a greater degree than Newton’s or any other (classical) theory.

In fact, even the most speculative of quantum theories of gravity obey this principle, as does string theory. Since in quantum mechanics, the behavior of systems is probabilistic, and not certain, it can happen that all of the known fundamental physical facts could, in theory, instantaneously change, in violation of our principle of self-consistency. This is the famous black hole information paradox, which is a major area of research in theoretical physics.

Another major motivation for string theory, indeed, is that it resolves this paradox. It does this by having enough degrees of freedom to encode all the information about a black hole into the light cones of its exterior. So, if gravity is not optional, then string theory is a very serious theory of quantum gravity, but if gravity is optional, then it is not necessarily as serious of a theory.

So, the question of whether gravity is optional, or not, is really a question of the self-consistency of a universe governed by such an optional gravitational law. output.text_basic:
What if we could have access to all of those memories and experiences whenever we wanted? What new directions might our knowledge and creativity take us?

These are the questions that drive the story in author K.L. Kolarich’s latest science fiction novel, “The Data Collectors.” Told in fast-moving segments that deftly build suspense and drama, the book explores the adventures of two protagonists who find themselves plunged headlong into a dangerous world.

Ari and her best friend, Roz, are high school sophomores who are thrilled to be accepted into an innovative science program for gifted teens at the local college. Under the direction of the brilliant and mysterious Dr. Rathburn, the teens are given small brain implants that they quickly discover allow them to store, retrieve, and share memories and experiences. But when an experiment goes horribly wrong, Ari and Roz are forced to go on the run as the doctors begin to take increasingly ominous steps to keep the girls quiet.

It turns out that the seemingly altruistic brain research project is actually a cover for a far more insidious plot. In the wrong hands, the brain implants and the database that they feed into could give governments and corporations the ability to control the thoughts and memories of entire populations – a scenario that has dark and often lethal consequences for the book’s main characters.

If you like adventure, brainteasers, science, and mystery (and, of course, a touch of romance), you will probably enjoy the high-speed twists and turns of “The Data Collectors.” Kolarich effectively conveys the fear, excitement, and anxiety that Ari and Roz feel as they are thrust into a grown-up world of secrets and betrayals. They are clever enough to outsmart their captors and protect each other, but not quite wise enough to understand the full implications of what they are doing.

The novel also features a nice balance of action, dialogue, and description to keep the plot moving rapidly along, a skill that more science fiction writers should master. Too often, the authors of this genre get so caught up in trying to explain the complexities of an imaginary world that they forget to give their characters personalities, motives, and voices. Kolarich’s two main characters have all of these qualities in spades, and they are easy to root for.

Another nice detail in the book is its setting. Much of the story takes place in a sleepy, small university town in the Midwest, and Kolarich does a good job of using the college atmosphere to add texture to the story. It could be any one of a thousand similar liberal arts colleges in the country, and you sense that Kolarich based the fictional school on some of her own college experiences.

I suppose a few diehard science fiction junkies will quibble about the minor details of the implants and data collection system that Kolarich creates in her novel, and they may be right to do so.

For most of us, however, “The Data Collectors” is a fast-paced and imaginative romp through a world that may not be so far off in our own future.

And who knows? It might even provoke you to take a closer look at your own brain someday.

output.text_basic:
This question lies at the heart of The Siren, the latest novel by Katherine St. John.

The novel begins with Stella, a 30-something year-old singer, drowning her sorrows in alcohol after her sister and manager, Lila, informs her that the band she’s part of is going to replace her since she’s no longer good enough. But before Stella can decide if she’d be better off alone or not, an alien presence descends and everyone, no matter their prior experience, wakes up able to sing perfectly.

The Siren is told from Stella’s perspective, and each chapter takes a look at how her newfound ability is affecting the lives of herself, her former bandmates and their manager–all while the news is trying to uncover what caused this phenomenon and what consequences it might have.

Overall, I loved The Siren. St. John writes with a clarity in her descriptions that make the book read as if you’re watching it unfold on television; she knows how to build action and tension; and her characters, as flawed as we are allowed to see as humans, feel real. You see them at their best, worst, weakest, strongest and every point in between.

## Answer (3)

It turns out that a simulation is almost certainly impossible; it's probably a violation of the laws of mathematics.

It's called Tegmark's level 4 multiverse. All simulations are fundamentally math, and there are some interesting results in set theory to the effect that there are very, very few *possible* simulation rules. I will now attempt to illustrate why.

There are infinity many integers. ℤ
There are a much larger infinity of real numbers. ℝ
There are even larger infinities! Cantor proved this, and his results are now part of the standard set theory foundation for all other math. Specifically, there exist larger infinities because
2^ℕ > ℕ

I'm going to make a slightly different statement, using these notations - a statement that, until we know for sure that the universe is a program, seems obviously not possible.
Everything is describable by the integers.

If you don't know math, you might look at that and ask what the hell the point is of defining a new field. After all, the integers describe everything, and you don't really need to worry about it. It seems trivial - if you don't know any better. The math is as follows:

ℤ == ℝ

That is "ℤ is equal to ℝ" - which is only true if there is a mapping from ℤ to ℝ and back again and always get the original real or integer back. I'm fairly sure we don't know whether this is possible, yet. At the very least, if it is possible the simulation would need to be *very* complex. (If you don't know math, this is more convincing; why? Just trust me that it's a lot more powerful than you think; the proof is in the link.)

But in general, you can say that a simulation, even if it could use more complicated things like ℝ, would have to be able to describe everything using less than something that is not possible for *us* to describe using *everything*.

A simulation would need to be able to do **all** of the math, even math that is so fundamentally difficult/complex that humans can't even *conceive* of how to begin answering those questions due to lack of physical equipment, even with a computer far more powerful than this planet's sun that runs forever and can run any program simultaneously.

Of course, this assumes the simulation is perfect (the set of all possible simulations), and there are a lot of good reasons to think this is the only one that might be able to even have a chance.

If you have some physical mechanism like, say, the laws of physics, you could conceivably have an advantage. But that's just a physical computer we can easily imagine. Why would someone go out of their way to build a physical computer and then simulate everything? The physical computer is *much* easier, and a physical computer cannot perform math any faster than that exact machine will allow (at base speed). While it's true the *program* could be massively faster than the physical computer, that is also true of a real-world computer.

In other words, the idea of simulation being possible is *hard* to accept until we know if the universe "itself" is a simulation. The "if" is doing a lot of work there, because a simulation and the actual universe have to have the same rules. If the universe is a computer, it's not likely to be a Windows computer; it's more likely to be a machine of some kind that we can't begin to comprehend.

In the end, the theory boils down to "If the universe is a physical machine, then it can be simulated by another machine that follows all the rules of the universe."

That doesn't sound very helpful, but remember that most mathematicians don't believe the universe is a machine. We don't know that the universe is one of the infinities that exist. There's no reason to assume something as simple as infinity-many atoms; it's possible we instead have infinity-many possible positions and configurations of *indistinguishable* particles. This is what the set theory foundation gets us - "It's not made of atoms, it's made of the infinities!" We know there are infinities. Is the universe based on those infinities, perhaps an infinity of possible quantum states? If so, what a bizarre universe we would live in, and we could not simulate that using classical computers! We would only be able to simulate things "slower" by using something that wasn't the universe itself!

In short, your assumption **might** have been wrong. If the universe *is* a machine, it's probably one we know nothing about.

Comment: Simulation Hypothesis is a bad theory for several reasons, I am not even sure it qualifies as a theory. It can't be verified or falsified, so it is unfalsifiable. If it can't be ruled out by facts, you can't say that it is true or false. It can't be tested, so it can't be proven. It is also tautological because it can't be falsified and can't be proven, it is unfalsifiable, the hypothesis itself doesn't imply anything since the concept of being in the Matrix is the same as just existing. Simulation Hypothesis can only tell us that our experience is real, but it can't tell us any truth.

## Answer (3)

It turns out that a simulation is almost certainly impossible; it's probably a violation of the laws of mathematics.

It's called Tegmark's level 4 multiverse. All simulations are fundamentally math, and there are some interesting results in set theory to the effect that there are very, very few *possible* simulation rules. I will now attempt to illustrate why.

There are infinity many integers. ℤ
There are a much larger infinity of real numbers. ℝ
There are even larger infinities! Cantor proved this, and his results are now part of the standard set theory foundation for all other math. Specifically, there exist larger infinities because
2^ℕ > ℕ

I'm going to make a slightly different statement, using these notations - a statement that, until we know for sure that the universe is a program, seems obviously not possible.
Everything is describable by the integers.

If you don't know math, you might look at that and ask what the hell the point is of defining a new field. After all, the integers describe everything, and you don't really need to worry about it. It seems trivial - if you don't know any better. The math is as follows:

ℤ == ℝ

That is "ℤ is equal to ℝ" - which is only true if there is a mapping from ℤ to ℝ and back again and always get the original real or integer back. I'm fairly sure we don't know whether this is possible, yet. At the very least, if it is possible the simulation would need to be *very* complex. (If you don't know math, this is more convincing; why? Just trust me that it's a lot more powerful than you think; the proof is in the link.)

But in general, you can say that a simulation, even if it could use more complicated things like ℝ, would have to be able to describe everything using less than something that is not possible for *us* to describe using *everything*.

A simulation would need to be able to do **all** of the math, even math that is so fundamentally difficult/complex that humans can't even *conceive* of how to begin answering those questions due to lack of physical equipment, even with a computer far more powerful than this planet's sun that runs forever and can run any program simultaneously.

Of course, this assumes the simulation is perfect (the set of all possible simulations), and there are a lot of good reasons to think this is the only one that might be able to even have a chance.

If you have some physical mechanism like, say, the laws of physics, you could conceivably have an advantage. But that's just a physical computer we can easily imagine. Why would someone go out of their way to build a physical computer and then simulate everything? The physical computer is *much* easier, and a physical computer cannot perform math any faster than that exact machine will allow (at base speed). While it's true the *program* could be massively faster than the physical computer, that is also true of a real-world computer.

In other words, the idea of simulation being possible is *hard* to accept until we know if the universe "itself" is a simulation. The "if" is doing a lot of work there, because a simulation and the actual universe have to have the same rules. If the universe is a computer, it's not likely to be a Windows computer; it's more likely to be a machine of some kind that we can't begin to comprehend.

In the end, the theory boils down to "If the universe is a physical machine, then it can be simulated by another machine that follows all the rules of the universe."

That doesn't sound very helpful, but remember that most mathematicians don't believe the universe is a machine. We don't know that the universe is one of the infinities that exist. There's no reason to assume something as simple as infinity-many atoms; it's possible we instead have infinity-many possible positions and configurations of *indistinguishable* particles. This is what the set theory foundation gets us - "It's not made of atoms, it's made of the infinities!" We know there are infinities. Is the universe based on those infinities, perhaps an infinity of possible quantum states? If so, what a bizarre universe we would live in, and we could not simulate that using classical computers! We would only be able to simulate things "slower" by using something that wasn't the universe itself!

In short, your assumption **might** have been wrong. If the universe *is* a machine, it's probably one we know nothing about.

output.text_basic:
The answer is almost impossible to determine, but that doesn't mean we can't try. In this article, we'll discuss some of the possibilities.

Losing your memory sounds like a nightmare, and it's not much easier if everybody forgets everything all at once. Let's take a look at a few scenarios and examine their potential effects.

If you happened to be sleeping during the moment that everyone forgot everything, you might be better off than those who experienced the memory loss directly. After all, you wouldn't know anything had changed. The rest of the world, however, would be in chaos. All of civilization's collective knowledge would be gone in an instant. People would forget how to read, write, build and grow food. The population would rapidly plummet, both from starvation and from violent conflict over scarce resources.

If you happened to be awake during the moment that everyone lost their memory, you'd be aware of the sudden shift in reality. If you could communicate with other people and form a cohesive group, you might be able to survive. However, group sizes would need to be small, since people might not remember how to cooperate or share. If there was some way to record your thoughts and observations, you might be able to preserve some knowledge for future generations. Even then, there's no telling how long it would take for human civilization to regain its former stature.

There's also the possibility that such a memory loss might not be permanent. For instance, if everyone was somehow able to regain their memories after a certain period of time passed, many or all of the effects that we've discussed might be reversed. If people were able to retain some long-term procedural memories, such as the habits and patterns that define their daily lives, then perhaps civilization could be rebuilt even if individual memories are lost.

However, this is all just speculation, and we should be grateful that such a phenomenon is unlikely to occur. Losing our memories would be a terrible fate for us as individuals and for humanity as a whole.

input.text_instructive: The Consequences Task. Your task is to imagine the consequences of an unusual situation. Please take your time to think creatively and provide as many responses as you can. Please list as many consequences as you can think of, considering various aspects such as personal, social, economic, and ethical implications. input.text_cot: What might be the implications if the Earth stopped rotating?Let's think step by step.

output.text_basic:
1. Days and Nights
The period of rotation of a planet determines the length of its day and night. On a planet similar to Earth, each rotation gives us a day and night cycle of approximately 12 hours each, making it 24 hours in total for a day. If Earth were to suddenly stop rotating, there would be no motion to distinguish day from night, thus making one side of the Earth eternally daylit while the other side would plunge into an eternal darkness.

2. Extreme Climates
The rotation of Earth also plays a crucial role in maintaining our planet's climate. It helps distribute heat evenly across the globe. Without this rotation, one side of the Earth would be scorching hot due to constant exposure to sunlight, while the other side would be extremely cold because of perpetual darkness. This drastic difference in temperature would make survival almost impossible.

3. Catastrophic Winds
As the Earth spins, it creates a Coriolis effect that influences wind patterns around the world. Without this rotation, wind patterns would change dramatically, leading to intense hurricanes and typhoons. Additionally, the absence of the Coriolis effect could result in straight-line winds which could cause significant damage.

4. Loss of Centrifugal Force
The spinning motion of the Earth creates a centrifugal force that keeps objects on the surface from falling towards the center. If Earth stopped rotating, this centrifugal force would disappear, resulting in everything being pulled towards the center. output.text_basic:
It’s a question that New York City–based startup Full Harvest is seeking to answer, in part, by raising $4 million in new funding to build out its platform for addressing food and plastic waste in the supply chain.

The new cash will come from Spark Capital, which led the round, and also Recycle Track Systems, an industrial and commercial trash removal company. Full Harvest’s existing investors also chipped in, including Wireframe Ventures, S2G Ventures, and the venture arm of the Campbell Soup Company.

Founded by former Cisco executive Christine Moseley, the startup created a business-to-business marketplace in 2015 to match growers of imperfect or surplus fruits and vegetables with large food companies that could resell the produce or use it in prepared foods and beverages.

Food wasted on farms costs U.S. growers more than $15 billion in lost revenue annually, while $218 billion is spent growing, processing, transporting, and disposing of food that will never be consumed, according to estimates from ReFED, which works with businesses, nonprofits, foundations, and government to reduce food waste.

And yet for all that lost value, fully 52% of food waste takes place in the consumer’s home. Another 40% happens at the commercial, industrial, and institutional level, while the remaining 8% is lost on farms, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.

To tackle that waste, Full Harvest is now setting its sights beyond ugly produce–its new platform enables food companies to buy and resell fruits and vegetables that are perfectly good but surplus to their needs. This could include, for instance, excess supplies of potatoes that supermarkets are overstocked with, or fruits and vegetables that don’t meet standards for certain customers.

But that’s not all the startup wants to do: Full Harvest has its eyes on a bigger prize–the $11.4 billion global market for plastic packaging used to wrap fruits and vegetables. The problem is that only about 14% of plastic packaging is recycled, and the rest ends up landfilled, or worse, in the ocean.

To that end, the company is working on creating a plastic that behaves like cardboard by using polylactic acid, a biodegradable material that can be derived from plant sugars and other organic materials, according to Moseley, the startup’s founder and CEO.  She first conceived of the idea while working in a Cisco networking closet under a desk piled high with plastic trash bins.

“That’s when I first realized how crazy the world’s reliance on plastic trash cans is,” Moseley said. ” They’re not just in one place. They’re at your schools, your offices, and your homes and they’re full of non-compostable, non-recyclable plastic bags.”

Since then Moseley realized that she could not just make a “better” plastic, but a plastic that biodegraded or turned into compost, like paper. With this new round of funding, the company is looking to work on a technology that could help its customers and partners transition from the $11.4 billion global plastic packaging market to one based on PLA, she said.

The reason this transition is so critical is because the amount of trash from industrial food and plastic waste that is going into landfills and clogging the environment is on the rise, according to a report from ReFED.

Using the UN Food and Agriculture Organization’s estimates that one third of food produced for human consumption is lost or wasted globally, and the World Resources Institute’s data on plastic use, ReFED estimates that the volume of food waste has increased by 50% since 1974. Meanwhile, plastic has increased by 200% since 1964, the report states.

That’s why Moseley is excited about a new partnership with the Campbell Soup Company (which is one of Full Harvest’s existing investors) and its subsidiary, Bolthouse Farms. The juice maker will start selling produce that is surplus or imperfect through Full Harvest to other Campbell soup businesses or on the marketplace, which will have already saved it from going to the landfill.

“We are really excited about this relationship,” Moseley said. “We believe it will be a springboard to a lot more growth.”

Ultimately, Full Harvest wants to build out its technologies and tools to help growers, food companies, logistics and supply chain firms, composters, recyclers, and plastic manufacturers work together to reduce food and plastic waste and transition to a system that uses biodegradable plastic, she said.

“We are looking to create a future where the industry works better,” Moseley said. “We want to use technology to reduce the massive amount of waste that is really bad for the environment and for our farmers’ bottom lines.”

Question: What would happen if plastic could biodegrade as quickly as paper?
Answer:  It’s a question that New York City–based startup Full Harvest is seeking to answer, in part, by raising $4 million in new funding to build out its platform for addressing food and plastic waste in the supply chain.

The new cash will come from Spark Capital, which led the round, and also Recycle Track Systems, an industrial and commercial trash removal company. Full Harvest’s existing investors also chipped in, including Wireframe Ventures, S2G Ventures, and the venture arm of the Campbell Soup Company.

Founded by former Cisco executive Christine Moseley, the startup created a business-to-business marketplace in 2015 to match growers of imperfect or surplus fruits and vegetables with large food companies that could resell the produce or use it in prepared foods and beverages.

Food wasted on farms costs U.S. growers more than $15 billion in lost revenue annually, while $218 billion is spent growing, processing, transporting, and disposing of food that will never be consumed, according to estimates from ReFED, which works with businesses, nonprofits, foundations, and government to reduce food waste.

And yet for all that lost value, fully 52% of food waste takes place in the consumer’s home. Another 40% happens at the commercial, industrial, and institutional level, while the remaining 8% is lost on farms, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.

To tackle that waste, Full Harvest is now setting its sights beyond ugly produce–its new platform enables food companies to buy and resell fruits and vegetables that are perfectly good but surplus to their needs. This could include, for instance, excess supplies of potatoes that supermarkets are overstocked with, or fruits and vegetables that don’t meet standards for certain customers.

But that’s not all the startup wants to do: Full Harvest has its eyes on a bigger prize–the $11.4 billion global market for plastic packaging used to wrap fruits and vegetables. The problem is that only about 14% of plastic packaging is recycled, and the rest ends up landfilled, or worse, in the ocean.

To that end, the company is working on creating a plastic that behaves like cardboard by using polylactic acid, a biodegradable material that can be derived from plant sugars and other organic materials, according to Moseley, the startup’s founder and CEO.  She first conceived of the idea while working in a Cisco networking closet under a desk piled high with plastic trash bins.

“That’s when I first realized how crazy the world’s reliance on plastic trash cans is,” Moseley said. ” They’re not just in one place. They’re at your schools, your offices, and your homes and they’re full of non-compostable, non-recyclable plastic bags.”

Since then Moseley realized that she could not just make a “better” plastic, but a plastic that biodegraded or turned into compost, like paper. With this new round of funding, the company is looking to work on a technology that could help its customers and partners transition from the $11.4 billion global plastic packaging market to one based on PLA, she said.

The reason this transition is so critical is because the amount of trash from industrial food and plastic waste that is going into landfills and clogging the environment is on the rise, according to a report from ReFED.

Using the UN Food and Agriculture Organization’s estimates that one third of food produced for human consumption is lost or wasted globally, and the World Resources Institute’s data on plastic use, ReFED estimates that the volume of food waste has increased by 50% since 1974. Meanwhile, plastic has increased by 200% since 1964, the report states.

That’s why Moseley is excited about a new partnership with the Campbell Soup Company (which is one of Full Harvest’s existing investors) and its subsidiary, Bolthouse Farms. The juice maker will start selling produce that is surplus or imperfect through Full Harvest to other Campbell soup businesses or on the marketplace, which will have already saved it from going to the landfill.

“We are really excited about this relationship,” Moseley said. “We believe it will be a springboard to a lot more growth.”

Ultimately, Full Harvest wants to build out its technologies and tools to help growers, food companies, logistics and supply chain firms, composters, recyclers, and plastic manufacturers work together to reduce food and plastic waste and transition to a system that uses biodegradable plastic, she said.

“We are looking to create a future where the industry works better,” Moseley said. “We want to use technology to reduce the massive amount of waste that is really bad for the environment and for our farmers’ bottom lines.”

output.text_basic:
The answer, as it turns out, would be interesting, unexpected, and downright bizarre. A newly published paper in the journal Demography sheds light on certain aspects of this scenario, using data from the past 250 years.

A group of demographers and economists, led by Jennifer B. Dowd at the University of Oxford, put together this study on how long-lived human populations would age. Using historical and contemporary data from Sweden, Denmark, and England and Wales, they determined that, if humans lived up to 200 years, we would not only live longer, but would give birth, have kids, and retire—all at different ages—compared to today, thanks to changes in life expectancy.

G/O Media may get a commission

“Our results show that many of the typical aging milestones, like retirement, would be pushed back much further into the life course if human lifespans increase dramatically,” said Dowd in a statement.

The team came to this conclusion by applying what are called “cohort-based period methods” to the historical and contemporary data, which allowed them to take into account the age at which events occur for certain cohorts of people—say, an 18-year-old and a 60-year-old—and how these timings would change in the future.

Increasing human lifespans by 50, 75, and 100 percent, the researchers found that, as lifespans increase, people would have their children later in life. Under these hypothetical scenarios, the mean age at parenthood would increase by 4 to 6 years. Currently, that number is about 28 years on average for developed countries. If lifespans increased to 200 years, the average age at parenthood would be around 40.

Under 100-year lifespans, people would spend a larger proportion of their lives in educational attainment and employment, and a smaller proportion in retirement. Once lifespan increases to 200 years, the age at retirement would start to decrease—though the researchers caution that this estimate is “likely to be higher than would actually be attained.”

Dowd doesn’t consider her study “prescriptive” or policy-focused, but it does offer a glimpse of what might be in store for society should human lifespans continue to increase.

“A few years ago, 50-year-old CEOs were a huge news item,” Dowd told Gizmodo. “Now it’s not even news—it’s a trend. As we extend healthy human lifespans, it’s inevitable that many of these milestones will shift later into life.”

There are obvious social and policy implications associated with these shifts, namely that life may be extended, but that time will have to be filled with something productive. In her work, Dowd says the “replacement rate”—the number of births per fertile women required to maintain the current population size—goes down as lifespans increase, so people will need to work longer to account for the larger retiree population. Aging populations, Dowd cautions, can cause labor market shortages and higher government spending on healthcare and aged-care, among other things.

Importantly, the study used data exclusively from three developed countries between 1800 and 2010, and the results may not apply to other kinds of countries and populations. For example, it’s unlikely that increasing longevity will have much of an impact in developing countries, at least for the foreseeable future, due to high levels of infectious disease and malnutrition. In Japan, where life expectancy is already exceedingly high, a 100-year lifespan hasn’t yet materialized; Japan’s average life expectancy is currently around 84.

And indeed, the researchers themselves don’t see the 100-year lifespan as a certainty.

“We cannot know whether the current exponential increase in human lifespan will continue,” the researchers write. That said, increasing lifespans is a distinct possibility, “and understanding their demographic consequences is of paramount importance.”

Increasing longevity, by itself, is not enough to ensure a healthy and equitable future; economic security, education, and healthcare are equally important. But this latest study offers a fascinating consideration of how much our lives would change should we start living significantly longer. And no amount of contemplation can take away from the sheer strangeness of contemplating a future in which humans live to 150 years, or even 200.

Question: What would happen if the average human lifespan increased to 200 years?
Answer:  The answer, as it turns out, would be interesting, unexpected, and downright bizarre. A newly published paper in the journal Demography sheds light on certain aspects of this scenario, using data from the past 250 years.

A group of demographers and economists, led by Jennifer B. Dowd at the University of Oxford, put together this study on how long-lived human populations would age. Using historical and contemporary data from Sweden, Denmark, and England and Wales, they determined that, if humans lived up to 200 years, we would not only live longer, but would give birth, have kids, and retire—all at different ages—compared to today, thanks to changes in life expectancy.

G/O Media may get a commission

“Our results show that many of the typical aging milestones, like retirement, would be pushed back much further into the life course if human lifespans increase dramatically,” said Dowd in a statement.

The team came to this conclusion by applying what are called “cohort-based period methods” to the historical and contemporary data, which allowed them to take into account the age at which events occur for certain cohorts of people—say, an 18-year-old and a 60-year-old—and how these timings would change in the future.

Increasing human lifespans by 50, 75, and 100 percent, the researchers found that, as lifespans increase, people would have their children later in life. Under these hypothetical scenarios, the mean age at parenthood would increase by 4 to 6 years. Currently, that number is about 28 years on average for developed countries. If lifespans increased to 200 years, the average age at parenthood would be around 40.

Under 100-year lifespans, people would spend a larger proportion of their lives in educational attainment and employment, and a smaller proportion in retirement. Once lifespan increases to 200 years, the age at retirement would start to decrease—though the researchers caution that this estimate is “likely to be higher than would actually be attained.”

Dowd doesn’t consider her study “prescriptive” or policy-focused, but it does offer a glimpse of what might be in store for society should human lifespans continue to increase.

“A few years ago, 50-year-old CEOs were a huge news item,” Dowd told Gizmodo. “Now it’s not even news—it’s a trend. As we extend healthy human lifespans, it’s inevitable that many of these milestones will shift later into life.”

There are obvious social and policy implications associated with these shifts, namely that life may be extended, but that time will have to be filled with something productive. In her work, Dowd says the “replacement rate”—the number of births per fertile women required to maintain the current population size—goes down as lifespans increase, so people will need to work longer to account for the larger retiree population. Aging populations, Dowd cautions, can cause labor market shortages and higher government spending on healthcare and aged-care, among other things.

Importantly, the study used data exclusively from three developed countries between 1800 and 2010, and the results may not apply to other kinds of countries and populations. For example, it’s unlikely that increasing longevity will have much of an impact in developing countries, at least for the foreseeable future, due to high levels of infectious disease and malnutrition. In Japan, where life expectancy is already exceedingly high, a 100-year lifespan hasn’t yet materialized; Japan’s average life expectancy is currently around 84.

And indeed, the researchers themselves don’t see the 100-year lifespan as a certainty.

“We cannot know whether the current exponential increase in human lifespan will continue,” the researchers write. That said, increasing lifespans is a distinct possibility, “and understanding their demographic consequences is of paramount importance.”

Increasing longevity, by itself, is not enough to ensure a healthy and equitable future; economic security, education, and healthcare are equally important. But this latest study offers a fascinating consideration of how much our lives would change should we start living significantly longer. And no amount of contemplation can take away from the sheer strangeness of contemplating a future in which humans live to 150 years, or even 200.
