output.text_basic:
The answer might be easier than you think. Just as a wilderness area manages their waste, you too can create “natural” areas to compost, with or without soil or composters.

When I visit a wilderness area, I am delighted to experience the pristine beauty of such a preserved space. Wilderness areas are protected and maintained for natural conditions to exist, leaving a footprint of native plant and animal ecosystems. There are no man-made structures in a wilderness area except for one exception—an outhouse.

When you visit an outhouse in a wilderness area, you will notice that there are often no toilets. There is usually just a wooden bench with a hole in it. To the side of the wooden bench is a slanted wooden box or a pile of ashes, which is the “toilet paper compost bin.” In other words, when you poop while camping, you don’t want to leave your waste where you pooped! You do this one of two ways: you either bury it with dirt/ashes or put it in the compost pile.

It wasn’t until I visited a wilderness area that I realized there was yet another method to deal with waste called humanure. Humanure is actually a book by Joseph C. Jenkins that explains this waste management concept in-depth. Humanure is human feces and urine and is a usable form of organic matter, which has been composted. Not only is this method helpful for campers, but many households also practice humanure recycling to reduce their trash and also improve the soil in their yards.

If you were to manage your waste without a trash can, a compost bin is an essential element. Compost bins can be as easy as building your own from scrap pieces of wood in your garage, purchasing a bin at your local home and garden store, or ordering a bin online from a company like the Humanure Handbook.

In addition to purchasing a composting bin, you will also need a small bucket with a lid, which will be your portable humanure collector. I would suggest that you place the bucket in your bathroom and cover the bucket with a toilet seat. The toilet seat will make it more comfortable for you or your family when depositing waste. Since you will be depositing urine and feces, it’s important to have a lid for the bucket because you don’t want anything inside the bucket to splash out onto your tile floor!

It is essential to collect a small amount of carbonaceous material (straw, sawdust, hay) to sprinkle in the bucket after each use. The carbonaceous material will help the waste break down more quickly, which will also deter the generation of unpleasant smells. The carbonaceous materials in the bucket will also help to neutralize odors.

When the bucket is full, you can empty it in your compost bin, which should be placed in a private area of your backyard. In order for the waste to break down, it must be covered with dirt from your garden. This method of covering the waste is called the “trenching method” or the “Berkley method,” which I learned from the Humanure Handbook.

There are no man-made structures in a wilderness area except for one exception—an outhouse.

When you visit an outhouse in a wilderness area, you will notice that there are often no toilets. There is usually just a wooden bench with a hole in it. To the side of the wooden bench is a slanted wooden box or a pile of ashes, which is the “toilet paper compost bin.” In other words, when you poop while camping, you don’t want to leave your waste where you pooped! You do this one of two ways: you either bury it with dirt/ashes or put it in the compost pile.

It wasn’t until I visited a wilderness area that I realized there was yet another method to deal with waste called humanure. Humanure is actually a book by Joseph C. Jenkins that explains this waste management concept in-depth. Humanure is human feces and urine and is a usable form of organic matter, which has been composted. Not only is this method helpful for campers, but many households also practice humanure recycling to reduce their trash and also improve the soil in their yards.

If you were to manage your waste without a trash can, a compost bin is an essential element. Compost bins can be as easy as building your own from scrap pieces of wood in your garage, purchasing a bin at your local home and garden store, or ordering a bin online from a company like the Humanure Handbook.

In addition to purchasing a composting bin, you will also need a small bucket with a lid, which will be your portable humanure collector. I would suggest that you place the bucket in your bathroom and cover the bucket with a toilet seat. The toilet seat will make it more comfortable for you or your family when depositing waste. Since you will be depositing urine and feces, it’s important to have a lid for the bucket because you don’t want anything inside the bucket to splash out onto your tile floor!

It is essential to collect a small amount of carbonaceous material (straw, sawdust, hay) to sprinkle in the bucket after each use. The carbonaceous material will help the waste break down more quickly, which will also deter the generation of unpleasant smells. The carbonaceous materials in the bucket will also help to neutralize odors.

When the bucket is full, you can empty it in your compost bin, which should be placed in a private area of your backyard. In order for the waste to break down, it must be covered with dirt from your garden. This method of covering the waste is called the “trenching method” or the “Berkley method,” which I learned from the Humanure Handbook.

At least once every three months, you should turn the compost pile to help the aerobic organisms break down the waste. Remember that the humanure recycling process can take up to a year. output.text_basic:
This question, posed in a survey as part of a research project, had a surprisingly high rate of failure.

A surprising number of respondents wrote: “I would go to the beach.”

Ironically, the survey sought to determine if people understand the amount of UV-B that is reaching their heads, and thus whether new products can help prevent head and neck skin cancer.

According to researchers, the results indicate that people fail to understand the amount of radiation that they are receiving on the top of their head.

> “It was a surprise at first,” said Brian Zelickson, MD, senior author of the paper and professor of dermatology at the Medical School.
> “Our intent was to find out if a UV detecting patch on a hat band might help people realize where the sun is shining, and to take better precautions.”

The survey was conducted on beach goers at popular beaches in California, Florida, and Virginia, asking respondents about their attitudes to sun, and how they would respond if they lost all their scalp hair.

Of the 216 women surveyed, 23.1% said they would go to the beach unprotected if they lost all their scalp hair, compared with only 6.4% of the 221 men surveyed.

Overall 17.8% of respondents, including 20.6% of females and 14.9% of males, reported they would go to the beach unprotected if they lost all their hair including their scalp.

In addition, only 27.2% of respondents, including 32.3% of females and 22.2% of males reported that they would use a UV protecting hat.

Researchers conclude that despite advances in public awareness of skin cancer caused by sunlight, a significant proportion of beach-goers would expose their scalp if all their hair was lost.

They suggest that new product designs will need to take into account how individuals perceive and take action to protect their heads from UV radiation in order to lower the rate of head and neck skin cancers.

The study is published in the journal Photodermatology, Photoimmunology & Photomedicine.

This question, posed in a survey as part of a research project, had a surprisingly high rate of failure.

> “It was a surprise at first,” said Brian Zelickson, MD, senior author of the paper and professor of dermatology at the Medical School.

Overall 17.8% of respondents, including 20.6% of females and 14.9% of males, reported they would go to the beach unprotected if they lost all their hair including their scalp.

In addition, only 27.2% of respondents, including 32.3% of females and 22.2% of males reported that they would use a UV protecting hat.

Researchers conclude that despite advances in public awareness of skin cancer caused by sunlight, a significant proportion of beach-goers would expose their scalp if all their hair was lost.

They suggest that new product designs will need to take into account how individuals perceive and take action to protect their heads from UV radiation in order to lower the rate of head and neck skin cancers.

output.text_basic:
The answer is simple but one most people overlook or neglect: You'd use fire-resistant materials in the construction and decor of your home. And there's another benefit: If you happen to live in an area frequented by termites or wood-boring insects, fire-resistant materials also resist insect damage. Not only will your home be fire safe, it will also be free of insect damage and, consequently, won't need pesticides. There are many fire-resistant materials on the market that are also attractive, long-lasting, and often more expensive because of the materials they contain or the way they're manufactured. But if you're on a limited budget, don't despair. Fire-resistant options exist that are also economical.

You may not realize it, but your home is probably built with fire-resistant materials that you never even think about. The fire-resistant materials your house is built with include the concrete or brick on the walls, the masonry filler around your windows, and the gypsum in your plasterboard and cement tiles. Any part of your home that is not protected by fire-resistant material is a potential source of danger. For example, exposed structural wood and wooden walls, floors, and ceilings are fuel for a fire. Even wooden cabinets can ignite during a fire and, once ignited, wood burns fast.

Because most wood-frame houses are built with fire-resistant materials, they have a higher degree of fire protection than people might think. For example, according to a report from the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, modern houses that suffer serious structural damage in fires are usually constructed with either insulated glass or plastic glazing around their doors -- or at least with single layer or uninsulated glass. Homes with either no glazing or with insulated glazing that includes metal frames and double-glazing tend to suffer less fire damage.

### Suggestions To Make Your Home More Fire-Resistant

If you are building a house or planning a major remodel, consult the many available books and articles on fire-resistive design and construction. In addition, there are several helpful sources you can turn to for more information on building or refurbishing your home with fire safety in mind. Local city building departments often have pamphlets or booklets with information on building fire-resistive structures; you can write to them for information. Several organizations and government agencies, such as the U.S. Government Accounting Office, conduct fire research and publish their findings. If you're looking for guidelines on how to build a home that can withstand a certain amount of heat and fire, the National Fire Protection Association can tell you what fire-resistance ratings apply to different building materials.

Even if you are not planning a major remodel, these are some suggestions that will make your home more fire resistant:

- If you are planning on replacing your roof, make sure that the new roof has a class-B or two-hour fire-resistance rating. Class-B roofs are covered with a noncombustible material such as asphalt, clay, slate, or concrete, and are rated to withstand a controlled laboratory spray fire test for 70 minutes. While a class-B rating does not guarantee that your roof will withstand actual fire, it does lower the potential for a fire to spread over the surface of your roof quickly.
- Keep the bushes and shrubs in your yard pruned so air can circulate more easily around and through them. Avoid placing wood piles or other flammables near your home.
- If you are replacing your windows and doors, be sure they are made of fire-resistant glazing. Double-glazed windows will help protect your home against heat as well as cold temperatures.
- Use fire-resistant drapes or shutters.
- Install smoke detectors.
- If you replace the eaves or trim of your house, or install new siding -- or if you are building a new home -- use fire-resistant materials rather than wood.
- Install interior walls that are at least one-half inch thick plasterboard, gypsum board, or similar fire-resistant material.
- Make any additions to your home from fire-resistant materials.
- Use metal, rather than wooden, ducts.
- Be sure that all wiring and electrical fixtures are hidden from view. Exposed wiring or electrical fixtures are easily damaged by fire.
- In wood structures, install sheet rock between the interior and exterior walls if they are less than ten feet apart. Sheet rock helps retard the spread of fire because it is highly absorbent, and it also insulates against heat.
- Avoid using carpeting in high-risk areas. If you do have wall-to-wall carpeting, make sure it is the low-flame-spread type; you can check with your carpet dealer or with the Carpet and Rug Institute.
- Store flammables securely in metal containers.

If you're concerned about fire safety -- and you should be -- then you should give serious thought to the use of fire-resistant materials. While many fire-resistant materials may be more expensive than those they replace, few home owners regret their purchases.

Question: If all fire-fighting equipment disappeared, how would you protect your home from a fire?
Answer:  The answer is simple but one most people overlook or neglect: You'd use fire-resistant materials in the construction and decor of your home. And there's another benefit: If you happen to live in an area frequented by termites or wood-boring insects, fire-resistant materials also resist insect damage. Not only will your home be fire safe, it will also be free of insect damage and, consequently, won't need pesticides. There are many fire-resistant materials on the market that are also attractive, long-lasting, and often more expensive because of the materials they contain or the way they're manufactured. But if you're on a limited budget, don't despair. Fire-resistant options exist that are also economical.

You may not realize it, but your home is probably built with fire-resistant materials that you never even think about. The fire-resistant materials your house is built with include the concrete or brick on the walls, the masonry filler around your windows, and the gypsum in your plasterboard and cement tiles. Any part of your home that is not protected by fire-resistant material is a potential source of danger. For example, exposed structural wood and wooden walls, floors, and ceilings are fuel for a fire. Even wooden cabinets can ignite during a fire and, once ignited, wood burns fast.

Because most wood-frame houses are built with fire-resistant materials, they have a higher degree of fire protection than people might think. For example, according to a report from the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, modern houses that suffer serious structural damage in fires are usually constructed with either insulated glass or plastic glazing around their doors -- or at least with single layer or uninsulated glass. Homes with either no glazing or with insulated glazing that includes metal frames and double-glazing tend to suffer less fire damage.

### Suggestions To Make Your Home More Fire-Resistant

If you are building a house or planning a major remodel, consult the many available books and articles on fire-resistive design and construction. In addition, there are several helpful sources you can turn to for more information on building or refurbishing your home with fire safety in mind. Local city building departments often have pamphlets or booklets with information on building fire-resistive structures; you can write to them for information. Several organizations and government agencies, such as the U.S. Government Accounting Office, conduct fire research and publish their findings. If you're looking for guidelines on how to build a home that can withstand a certain amount of heat and fire, the National Fire Protection Association can tell you what fire-resistance ratings apply to different building materials.

Even if you are not planning a major remodel, these are some suggestions that will make your home more fire resistant:

- If you are planning on replacing your roof, make sure that the new roof has a class-B or two-hour fire-resistance rating. Class-B roofs are covered with a noncombustible material such as asphalt, clay, slate, or concrete, and are rated to withstand a controlled laboratory spray fire test for 70 minutes. While a class-B rating does not guarantee that your roof will withstand actual fire, it does lower the potential for a fire to spread over the surface of your roof quickly.
- Keep the bushes and shrubs in your yard pruned so air can circulate more easily around and through them. Avoid placing wood piles or other flammables near your home.
- If you are replacing your windows and doors, be sure they are made of fire-resistant glazing. Double-glazed windows will help protect your home against heat as well as cold temperatures.
- Use fire-resistant drapes or shutters.
- Install smoke detectors.
- If you replace the eaves or trim of your house, or install new siding -- or if you are building a new home -- use fire-resistant materials rather than wood.
- Install interior walls that are at least one-half inch thick plasterboard, gypsum board, or similar fire-resistant material.
- Make any additions to your home from fire-resistant materials.
- Use metal, rather than wooden, ducts.
- Be sure that all wiring and electrical fixtures are hidden from view. Exposed wiring or electrical fixtures are easily damaged by fire.
- In wood structures, install sheet rock between the interior and exterior walls if they are less than ten feet apart. Sheet rock helps retard the spread of fire because it is highly absorbent, and it also insulates against heat.
- Avoid using carpeting in high-risk areas. If you do have wall-to-wall carpeting, make sure it is the low-flame-spread type; you can check with your carpet dealer or with the Carpet and Rug Institute.
- Store flammables securely in metal containers.

If you're concerned about fire safety -- and you should be -- then you should give serious thought to the use of fire-resistant materials. While many fire-resistant materials may be more expensive than those they replace, few home owners regret their purchases.

According to the 2017 Census of Governments, states like Idaho, California, and Kentucky have reported that over half of their 2016-2017 public schools closed due to extreme weather conditions.

When it snows or gets too cold, when wind speeds reach over 100 mph, or when lightning strikes are too intense, public schools across our country can be shut down for days due to infrastructural incapabilities.

It is for this reason that we need to equip our schools with more technologically advanced infrastructure so that they can not only educate children but also protect our most valuable resource that is also our future.

Incorporating technology in schools not only provides students with the resources and opportunities to be prepared for the 21st century, but it also allows children to be educated during disasters.

One form of such infrastructure that can be implemented into public schools is interactive displays. Interactive displays are large touch-screen monitors that can be connected to the internet or local networks and allow multiple users to engage with the material being displayed, increasing collaboration and engagement in the classroom.

Interactive Displays vs Paper-Based Learning

One argument in favor of implementing interactive displays is that “touch technology” is the preferred method of communication for younger generations.

As touch screen use and smartphone usage grows increasingly prevalent in our society, people from the ages of 5 to 25 have been more accustomed to using touch technology rather than pen and paper.

Research has shown that the use of touchscreen technology in education aids in student motivation, engagement and overall performance.

In the digital age where information is exchanged at such a rapid pace, technology in schools can allow students to access information quicker and more efficiently than paper-based learning.

Interactive displays can allow students to easily search for information from all around the world, allowing them to gather multiple perspectives on a topic so that they can have more informed and engaging class discussions that can challenge their thinking and promote the development of critical thinking and empathetic skills.

Interactive displays also help in fostering problem-solving abilities.

One of the major differences between interactive displays and paper-based learning is that interactive displays allow for multi-sensory learning which can help students to better understand complex concepts.

Interactive displays also help in saving costs in the long term and are less likely to break compared to other teaching equipment.

Paper-based learning contributes to higher costs since they require the frequent purchase of textbooks and paper materials that get easily damaged; whereas interactive touchscreen displays can have a lifespan of up to 10 years if properly maintained.

Moreover, interactive displays decrease the likelihood of classroom damage since students are physically touching a screen instead of pulling apart the pages of a book.

Interactive Displays vs Whiteboards

Interactive displays have several advantages over traditional whiteboards:

Interactive displays have a larger screen size than tradition whiteboards. Having a larger screen size allows teachers to project more detailed materials and for more students to see what is being projected at the same time.

Moreover, interactive displays are easier to view at different angles compared to traditional whiteboards. This is because the touchscreen display technology used in interactive displays is designed to allow users to view the contents of the screen without having to be directly in front of the screen, which increases engagement and allows teachers to walk around the class without having to worry about classroom seating arrangements.

Interactive displays also have higher resolution than whiteboards. Higher resolution allows teachers to project more detailed images which can help students to better understand complex concepts.

Another advantage of interactive displays is that they can easily connect into a network. Being connected to a network allows teachers to save their material and share it with their colleagues or with other teachers, so that they can share materials.

This also allows students to easily access their teachers’ material by using their mobile devices to link their work to the display, helping them to have more informed and engaging class discussions.

Lastly, because interactivity is a feature that is integrated into the screen, the quality of penmanship does not deteriorate over time. However, with whiteboards, the quality of penmanship can depreciate over time since the whiteboard markers can run out of ink, which can lead to illegible writing.

With an interactive display, writing and drawing is a more effective method since the display provides the functionality of writing on the display screen with the ease and convenience of a keyboard and mouse, thus eliminating the issue of poor penmanship.

Disasters and Educational Continuity

The United States experiences over 1,300 tornadoes and 30,000 wildfires per year; events that can leave communities with damaged schools, and thus, a discontinuity in children’s education.

Since schools serve more than just education—they also provide students with free lunches and a place for students to be supervised and cared for while their parents are at work—discontinuity in education can have devastating effects on the development of a community.

According to the 2017 Annual Homeless Assessment Report to Congress, over 40,000 children and unaccompanied minors were homeless in California, Idaho, and Kentucky due to the loss of their homes in the wake of tornadoes and fires.

With interactive displays, classrooms can be digitally managed so that teachers can deliver lectures remotely.

If schools are physically damaged by disasters and forced to close, interactive displays can be used to facilitate online learning since teachers can connect their materials to an online database that students can access using their mobile devices.

If there is a power outage in the area, interactive displays can also be used offline since they can be equipped with batteries.

When a disaster occurs, power outages and infrastructure disruptions can cause problems in a community's internet connection.

This is exactly why interactive displays can also come with software that allows students to work offline by saving the display content onto an application that works offline as well, allowing students to complete their work and transfer it to a portable storage device or print their work.

Interactive displays are an easy, economical way to ensure that children have access to resources that can help them to be prepared for the future that awaits them.

By implementing interactive displays in schools, there will be an increase in student engagement, motivation, and performance.

Moreover, teachers will be better equipped to manage their classrooms and to respond to emergency situations; thus, providing the potential for schools to create a generation of intelligent, informed, and critical-thinking future leaders that will be able to deal with the challenges of the 21st and beyond.

You'd need

1. A teacher,
2. Some tools (books, videos, or online resources),
3. A place to teach (home, community space, etc.).

This is precisely what homeschooling offers. Homeschoolers (parents and/or guardians) assume the role of the teacher, and the family's home, library, internet, etc., will form the learning environment. Home education may be a good fit for some of you looking for alternatives to traditional education. Here's a quick homeschooling guide to help you.

## Is Homeschooling Legal?

Almost all states allow homeschooling. However, there may be a set of rules and regulations you need to follow. You can find information about the homeschooling laws specific to your state through the Home School Legal Defense Association or HSLDA.

## Benefits of Homeschooling

Researchers have looked at the relative social, emotional, academic, and other development of homeschooled children and conventionally schooled children. Here is a summary of the findings.

### Socialization

While homeschoolers do not receive as much social interaction with peers outside the home compared to conventionally schooled children, this does not translate to issues with socialization. In fact, the evidence suggests the opposite. A review of the research evidence on homeschooling and socialization found that:

- "Although homeschooled children spend a significant amount of time with their parents and siblings, they have frequent opportunities to interact with adults and children outside their family."
- "Studies show that peer relationships for homeschooled children are very positive. Homeschooled children are largely socially integrated and have well-developed social skills."
- Homeschooled children "do not appear to experience negative socialization effects."

### Academic Achievement

Evidence shows that homeschoolers do at least as well as the average conventionally schooled child on standardized tests. Another meta-analysis of the standardized test scores of homeschooled students found:

- Homeschooled children "obtain significantly higher scores than their public school counterparts."
- "The homeschooled students’ achievement scores were consistently above average."

### Other Findings About Homeschooled Students

- They "have developed a highly positive self-image."
- They show "more mature and pro-social behaviors than their conventionally schooled counterparts."
- "They express curiosity and interests more frequently and display fewer signs of psychological distress."
- "Homeschooled students have better moral values and demonstrate less interest in activities such as substance abuse, violent behavior, and early sexual behavior." "These students have a higher degree of tolerance for racial and religious minorities, and are more likely to stand up for students being harassed or bullied."

Overall, the evidence suggests that homeschoolers benefit greatly from the learning approach, which provides them with a supportive, positive, and empowering learning environment.

## How to Homeschool: 10 Basic Steps

1. Research homeschool laws in your state. You can visit Home School Legal Defense Association (HSLDA) and search "how to start homeschooling in [your state]" for a step-by-step guide on homeschooling laws in your state.
2. Set educational goals for your children. Decide on the purpose of homeschooling, your desired homeschool curriculum, and your expectations for homeschooling children in grades K-12 or below.
3. Decide on a homeschool curriculum. Choose a curriculum that meets your educational goals and is suitable for your children based on age, interests, and learning style. Some options for homeschoolers include public school programs, religious programs, and secular programs.
4. Choose a homeschooling method. Find a homeschooling method that is best for your family. Options may include:
    - Traditional: You teach the subjects that the public school would typically teach using the provided curriculum or one that you choose.
    - Unit studies: You teach different academic subjects while focusing on one topic at a time. Use materials like textbooks, novels, videos, and more.
    - Charlotte Mason: You focus on providing children with living books, first-hand experiences, and more.
    - Worldschooling: You travel the world with your children while learning about various places, cultures, and histories.
    - Eclectic: You can choose any method of homeschooling that fits your family and choose the curriculum and teaching methods you prefer.
5. Create a homeschool schedule. You can create a flexible schedule that suits your family's needs. This schedule might consist of 1-4 hours per day, five days per week. You can choose to homeschool in the morning or afternoon, on weekdays or weekends.
6. Register your homeschool. In most states, you will need to register as a homeschool, which usually involves filling out a form or sending in a notice of intent.
7. Understand record-keeping requirements. Many states have specific record-keeping requirements for homeschoolers. Visit your state's homeschooling laws to understand the requirements in your location.
8. Plan for extracurricular activities. Plan for extracurricular activities like sports, music lessons, clubs, volunteer work, community service, internships, and more to help your children grow personally and socially.
9. Find a homeschool group. Look for local homeschool groups, co-ops, or support groups that can help you plan field trips, sports activities, and social events with your children and their peers.
10. Be open to experimenting. Be open to trying out different methods of homeschooling, different curricula, and new ways of teaching your children. This will help you find the right balance for your family and keep your homeschool experience positive and enjoyable.

2. Rudner, Lawrence M. (1999). Scholastic achievement and demographic characteristics of home school students in 1998. Educational Policy Analysis Archives 7(8), 1-39.
3. Duvall, Jill Wade. (2019). Is homeschooling an effective and healthy educational alternative? Pediatric Annals 48(6), e244-e250.
4. Martin-Chang, S., Gould, O. N., & Meuse, R. (2011). A comparative study of the academic achievement and attitudes of home schooled and traditionally schooled students. Journal of School Psychology 49(4), 527-545.

Question: If all schools were to suddenly close, how would you educate children? Let's think step by step.
Answer:  You'd need

1. A teacher,
2. Some tools (books, videos, or online resources),
3. A place to teach (home, community space, etc.).

This is precisely what homeschooling offers. Homeschoolers (parents and/or guardians) assume the role of the teacher, and the family's home, library, internet, etc., will form the learning environment. Home education may be a good fit for some of you looking for alternatives to traditional education. Here's a quick homeschooling guide to help you.

## Is Homeschooling Legal?

Almost all states allow homeschooling. However, there may be a set of rules and regulations you need to follow. You can find information about the homeschooling laws specific to your state through the Home School Legal Defense Association or HSLDA.

## Benefits of Homeschooling

Researchers have looked at the relative social, emotional, academic, and other development of homeschooled children and conventionally schooled children. Here is a summary of the findings.

### Socialization

While homeschoolers do not receive as much social interaction with peers outside the home compared to conventionally schooled children, this does not translate to issues with socialization. In fact, the evidence suggests the opposite. A review of the research evidence on homeschooling and socialization found that:

- "Although homeschooled children spend a significant amount of time with their parents and siblings, they have frequent opportunities to interact with adults and children outside their family."
- "Studies show that peer relationships for homeschooled children are very positive. Homeschooled children are largely socially integrated and have well-developed social skills."
- Homeschooled children "do not appear to experience negative socialization effects."

### Academic Achievement

Evidence shows that homeschoolers do at least as well as the average conventionally schooled child on standardized tests. Another meta-analysis of the standardized test scores of homeschooled students found:

- Homeschooled children "obtain significantly higher scores than their public school counterparts."
- "The homeschooled students’ achievement scores were consistently above average."

### Other Findings About Homeschooled Students

- They "have developed a highly positive self-image."
- They show "more mature and pro-social behaviors than their conventionally schooled counterparts."
- "They express curiosity and interests more frequently and display fewer signs of psychological distress."
- "Homeschooled students have better moral values and demonstrate less interest in activities such as substance abuse, violent behavior, and early sexual behavior." "These students have a higher degree of tolerance for racial and religious minorities, and are more likely to stand up for students being harassed or bullied."

Overall, the evidence suggests that homeschoolers benefit greatly from the learning approach, which provides them with a supportive, positive, and empowering learning environment.

## How to Homeschool: 10 Basic Steps

1. Research homeschool laws in your state. You can visit Home School Legal Defense Association (HSLDA) and search "how to start homeschooling in [your state]" for a step-by-step guide on homeschooling laws in your state.
2. Set educational goals for your children. Decide on the purpose of homeschooling, your desired homeschool curriculum, and your expectations for homeschooling children in grades K-12 or below.
3. Decide on a homeschool curriculum. Choose a curriculum that meets your educational goals and is suitable for your children based on age, interests, and learning style. Some options for homeschoolers include public school programs, religious programs, and secular programs.
4. Choose a homeschooling method. Find a homeschooling method that is best for your family. Options may include:
    - Traditional: You teach the subjects that the public school would typically teach using the provided curriculum or one that you choose.
    - Unit studies: You teach different academic subjects while focusing on one topic at a time. Use materials like textbooks, novels, videos, and more.
    - Charlotte Mason: You focus on providing children with living books, first-hand experiences, and more.
    - Worldschooling: You travel the world with your children while learning about various places, cultures, and histories.
    - Eclectic: You can choose any method of homeschooling that fits your family and choose the curriculum and teaching methods you prefer.
5. Create a homeschool schedule. You can create a flexible schedule that suits your family's needs. This schedule might consist of 1-4 hours per day, five days per week. You can choose to homeschool in the morning or afternoon, on weekdays or weekends.
6. Register your homeschool. In most states, you will need to register as a homeschool, which usually involves filling out a form or sending in a notice of intent.
7. Understand record-keeping requirements. Many states have specific record-keeping requirements for homeschoolers. Visit your state's homeschooling laws to understand the requirements in your location.
8. Plan for extracurricular activities. Plan for extracurricular activities like sports, music lessons, clubs, volunteer work, community service, internships, and more to help your children grow personally and socially.
9. Find a homeschool group. Look for local homeschool groups, co-ops, or support groups that can help you plan field trips, sports activities, and social events with your children and their peers.
10. Be open to experimenting. Be open to trying out different methods of homeschooling, different curricula, and new ways of teaching your children. This will help you find the right balance for your family and keep your homeschool experience positive and enjoyable.

output.text_basic:
If your legs didn't work, how would you go far?  Who would you tell your secrets to if there was no one left to trust?

My son asked me questions like these in the car a few days ago.  At the time, I really had no idea where the curiosity came from but I happily answered him with the most basic of logic and reasoning.  In my mind they were little kid questions so I should answer in kind, right?

Apparently not.  He had been given the questions from his school and was required to answer them in writing.  He also had to answer a handful of questions about himself- Who do you think makes the best pizza in the world?  Who would you invite to your birthday party if you could invite anyone?  Who is your best friend?  If you could choose a world record to break, what would it be?

It didn't take long for this assignment to get me thinking.

I would say that I'm more than a little obsessed with asking questions of myself.  I do it all the live long day.  Most of them have something to do with my children and some variation of what I should feed them next, what kind of activities they need for the week, how should I balance school schedules with housekeeping schedules, when and how often should they be allowed screen time and whether or not ice cream is a proper meal replacement.

More often than not, these questions are pretty surface level.

And, yes, while it is important, perhaps even more important, to take care of the physical needs of my children, it occurred to me that perhaps I might benefit from asking myself some deeper questions, just like my son.

Intrigued?  I was!

So I have written a list of 50 questions.  Some of them are serious, some are silly and fun, but all of them are worth considering.

If you'd like to join me in answering these questions, feel free to copy, type or write them yourself and spend some time on them this week.

I promise you won't regret it!

1. What makes me the happiest?

2. What is my biggest fear?

3. Who in my life brings me the greatest joy?

4. What is my biggest regret?

5. What is the first book that made me cry?

6. If I could have any super power, what would it be?

7. If I could travel back in time, where would I go?

8. What is one thing I do that always brings a smile to my face?

9. If I could choose one song to be my anthem, what would it be?

10. One year from now, what do I want to be able to say that I have accomplished?

11. How many times a week do I workout?  Is it enough?

12. Who do I most enjoy cooking for?

13. When is the last time I sent a letter by mail?

14. What do I miss most about being a child?

15. What part of myself do I need to work on most?

16. What is it that keeps me up at night?

17. Do I say and show my love often enough?

18. What do I need to work on to be kinder?

19. When was the last time I had an adventure?

20. What do I wish was easier?

21. Why am I grateful for the family I was born in to?

22. Why am I grateful for the family I have created?

23. What 5 things do I want to teach my children the most?

24. What is my favorite kind of fruit?

25. What is my favorite dessert?

26. What is the most adventurous thing I've ever done?

27. Is there someone that I need to forgive?

28. Is there someone that needs to forgive me?

29. One thing I would never give up on?

30. One thing that I would try really hard to do without giving up?

31. What do I see as my role is the world?

32. What do I see as my role within my family?

33. What is the best thing about being me?

34. When is the last time I had my life flash before my eyes?

35. If I could choose one thing to redo, what would it be?

36. At what age did I feel most content?

37. What is my favorite thing to grow in my yard?

38. Why did I choose the profession I am in?

39. If I had the power to ban one thing from the earth, what would it be?

40. What is one thing that I would do if I wasn't afraid?

41. What is my favorite hobby?

42. When I think about death, it scares me because _______

43. What is one thing that I wouldn't mind being remembered for?

44. What is one thing that I would regret being remembered for?

45. If I could have dinner with anyone in the world, who would it be and why?

46. What is one thing that most people don't know about me?

47. What is one thing that I could do to make this world a better place?

48. What is another thing that I could do to make this world a better place?

49. What is the most important thing that I could do to make myself happier?

50. If I could go back in time and give myself one piece of advice, what would it be?

Now, answer me this question...  Do you feel like you are a better person having reflected on these questions?  If you do, and I hope you did, isn't that a wonderful thing?

Spend as much time answering these questions as you would like.  Perhaps you'd like to break them up into several days or just set aside a couple of hours one evening.  If you take anything away from this list, I hope you feel a sense of growth and development that has come from answering these questions.  Perhaps you have discovered something new about yourself.  Maybe you have learned that your perspective has changed and you've recognized that in yourself.

Maybe you have realized that you are not the person you would like to be, but that's OK, too.

You are working on it; keep working on it.

I know that I was glad to have spent the time asking myself these simple questions, and I have also discovered quite a lot about myself in the process.

That's all for today.

And thank you so much for sharing a part of your day with me.

Until tomorrow, my friends... xo

output.text_basic:
Many survival cookbooks focus on finding or using campfires and other outdoor cooking strategies, but with modern preparedness in mind, you could set out to stock up what you need for an indoor cooking arrangement.

Preparing an indoor cooking arrangement with minimal or no actual cooking equipment isn’t as difficult or as unhealthy as one might think. With a few simple steps, your food storage preparation can also include a few items for preserving the food and turning it into meals.

First, let’s talk about cooking with absolutely nothing. Most people know the old Boy Scout way of using rocks, a small pit, and branches to create a small campfire. After a few matches have been used to ignite the fire, it can be stoked and fed to a healthy blaze within a matter of minutes. A cast iron dutch oven or foil-lined pan can be held over the fire to cook most anything without much difficulty.

The same process can be used indoors using a very small barbecue grill. If you have a terrace or sun porch, an old-fashioned grate can hold a pan over the fire to cook whatever you are making.  If you don’t have a grate, you can place a rock or two to hold the pan level. Obviously, you should not rely on this arrangement alone or create one without first assuring yourself that it will not send smoke or fumes into the main part of the house.

An alternative method that has been used for hundreds of years, is cooking over a small woodstove. Many homesteaders used this method to cook food and preserve the warmth during winter. While the large cast iron stove with a warmer and oven may be impractical for the small amount of cooking expected during an emergency, a small woodstove can certainly be useful.

Alternatively, you could invest in a small catalytic or propane gas stove for indoor cooking. These appliances are not as expensive as many people might think and they can be purchased for use with your present gas line or propane tanks. They are fairly easy to install and they can provide a large amount of power for cooking and even boiling water over an open flame. These appliances have the added benefit of being fairly safe to use indoors, as they will not generate smoke.

If you’re lucky enough to have natural gas, you can purchase a gas powered blender that can be used indoors to cook almost anything. This is a great alternative to the old method of using a blender or a mortar and pestle to grind ingredients into a thick batter for making a tasty stew.

If a natural disaster strikes and you find yourself unable to leave your house, but with a plentiful food supply, you can certainly make good use of your food storage. The key is to be prepared ahead of time. Start by stocking up a few things that can be used to cook indoors, even if it’s just a small grate and some matches.

You can always add to your indoor cooking arrangement as you go, such as a small catalytic or propane gas stove. When it comes to preparing meals during a disaster, you can never have too many options available to you.

output.text_basic:
A question like that makes you think about the Earth’s ecosystem.

As a global community, it’s time to take better care of the world we live in. And, what better way to do that than by learning about the environment in science?

Today, we explore various types of activities in science class that will make your students more environmentally conscious. Get your lesson plans ready!

## 1. Environmental Studies

Environmental studies are an umbrella term that includes several branches of science. From biology to physics and social studies, environmental science pulls from various disciplines.

At its core, environmental science is all about understanding our relationship with and responsibility to the natural world.

It examines environmental concerns through the lens of social and political science. This means it encourages students to think critically about the complex relationship between ecological systems and human activity.

You can find several different environmental studies programs for your classroom. For example, there is an Introduction to Ecology course that centers on the study of living creatures and their relationship with one another and the earth.

The lesson plans for this course could include various lab or field experiments. Students could examine the ecosystem of a local park, learn about water and soil chemistry, and study the effects of habitat distruction.

## 2. Compost Projects

Composting is an excellent way to introduce some elementary concepts in biology and chemistry. A compost project shows students the benefits of recycling organic matter.

Composting reduces the amount of waste that heads straight for the landfill. It also converts organic waste into useful, nutrient-rich fertilizer for plants.

This can be a long-term project that spans multiple weeks. For example, you could make class trips to a garden bed on the school grounds. Alternatively, you can set up a compost bin in the back of the classroom for students to manage.

The compost pile is an ideal setting for hands-on lessons in science. Here are several science concepts you can cover with compost activities:

- Decomposition
- Microbiology (microbes)
- Chemical reactions (carbon, decomposing)
- Soil nutrients
- Plant systems

## 3. Pollution Prevention Experiments

Pollution is a big issue that requires immediate attention. A pollution prevention project helps students develop their critical thinking skills while learning about real-world problems.

You can start with an introductory discussion on the three types of pollution. This includes air pollution, water pollution, and soil pollution.

Then, you can have students research a case study of a specific type of pollution. A local pollutant is most relevant, but you can also use global situations for case studies.

As part of their research, students could visit a polluted site to collect data and water samples. They then analyze laboratory results to understand the extent of the damage.

This makes for a great cross-curricular activity. For example, students could write essays in their English class about the environmental justice topic they learn about in science. In history class, students could explore political actions taken regarding the polluted site.

## 4. Carbon Footprint

Carbon footprints are measures of carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere as a result of human activity. This could be in the form of fuel consumption, waste disposal, and the use of manufactured goods.

A fun activity for your science classes is to have students measure their carbon footprints by calculating their CO2 emissions.

Your students can estimate their carbon footprints based on their daily habits. For example, factors that affect carbon emissions include the type of vehicle people drive, the type of energy they use at home, and the transportation mode they use to get to school.

Once they’ve calculated their CO2 emissions, students can take various steps to reduce the size of their footprint. They can explore the possibility of:

- Using public transportation or carpooling to school
- Adopting green energy sources (solar or wind power)
- Reducing water waste by turning off the faucet while brushing their teeth
- Using a refillable water bottle instead of buying plastic bottles
- Shopping at local farmers’ markets instead of buying from big-box stores

## 5. Greenhouse Gas Experiments

Carbon footprints and greenhouse gases go hand-in-hand. A greenhouse gas experiment would be an excellent way for your students to explore the science behind global warming.

Step 1: Understand the Role of Animals
Animals, including insects, play a crucial role in the ecosystem. They help control pest populations through predation, parasitism, and competition. For example, birds, bats, and spiders consume tons of insects every day. Without them, insect populations could explode.

Step 2: Evaluate Current Pest Control Methods
Currently, we use various methods to control pests, such as chemical pesticides, traps, and biological controls like ladybugs that eat aphids. However, these methods have limitations and can sometimes cause harm to non-target species or the environment.

Step 3: Explore Alternative Solutions
If animals were to disappear, we would need to explore alternative solutions for pest control. Here are some possibilities:

- Genetic modification: We could genetically modify crops to be resistant to pests or release genetically modified male insects that cannot reproduce.
- Robots: Autonomous robots could be developed to detect and kill pests or harvest crops.
- Nanotechnology: Nanoparticles could be used to deliver pesticides directly to pests, reducing harm to non-target species.
- Synthetic biology: Scientists could create synthetic organisms that perform specific tasks, such as consuming pests or producing beneficial compounds.

Step 4: Consider the Risks and Benefits
Each alternative solution has its own risks and benefits. For example, genetic modification could lead to unintended consequences, while robots and nanotechnology could be expensive and energy-intensive. Synthetic biology raises ethical concerns and could potentially create new risks.

Step 5: Implement a Multi-Pronged Approach
A combination of different strategies would likely be the most effective approach for pest control in the absence of animals. This could include a mix of genetic modification, robots, nanotechnology, and synthetic biology, along with integrated pest management practices such as crop rotation and habitat modification.

In conclusion, if animals were to disappear, we would need to explore alternative solutions for pest control. While this presents challenges and risks, it also offers opportunities for innovation and creativity in solving one of humanity's oldest problems.

Let's think about vitamin D deficiency from space...
The sun rises over the earth every morning, illuminating every part of our planet in a blanket of soft light. Many of our daily activities, including eating, working, and playing, are influenced by the availability of sunlight. Even after sundown, we often rely on artificial lighting to help us complete our daily tasks.

However, there are parts of our planet where sunlight is not as readily available, such as the Arctic and Antarctic regions – areas that experience extended periods of darkness during the winter months. In these regions, it can be difficult to get enough sunlight to meet the body's daily needs for vitamin D.

Vitamin D is a vital nutrient that is essential for the maintenance of healthy bones and teeth. It is also important for the proper functioning of the immune system and for the regulation of mood and energy levels. Although we can get vitamin D from certain foods, such as fatty fish and fortified dairy products, the best source of vitamin D is sunlight.

The skin produces vitamin D when it is exposed to ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation from the sun. This process, known as photoproduction, occurs within minutes of sun exposure. However, there are several factors that can influence the body's ability to produce vitamin D from sunlight, including the time of day, the season, the latitude, and the amount of cloud cover.

In cloudy conditions, the amount of UVB radiation that reaches the earth's surface is reduced, making it more difficult for the skin to produce vitamin D. This can lead to vitamin D deficiency, a condition that affects millions of people around the world.

Vitamin D deficiency can have serious consequences for health, including increased risk of osteoporosis, fractures, and falls in older adults. It has also been linked to a higher risk of certain cancers, autoimmune disorders, and cardiovascular disease.

To prevent vitamin D deficiency, it is important to consume enough vitamin D-rich foods and to get enough sunlight exposure. This can be challenging, particularly during the winter months, when the availability of sunlight is limited.

For people living in regions with prolonged periods of cloud cover, it may be necessary to take vitamin D supplements to ensure that they are getting enough of this essential nutrient. Talk to your doctor or a registered dietitian to determine the best way to meet your vitamin D needs.

output.text_basic:
You wouldn't be able to buy or sell anything, yet human needs and wants would persist. To fulfill them, we'd have some sort of barter system. That's a system where each person or group provides something to others in exchange for getting something they need from them. A classic barter example is a farmer and a baker. The baker bakes bread every day, and the farmer grows beans. The farmer needs bread and the baker needs beans, so they exchange goods. In ancient times, when currency was first introduced, bartering was a common way to survive.

When the economy crashed in 2008, bartering rose in popularity. As people worried about how they could afford what they need, they searched for creative ways to get what they wanted without using money.

Care to learn more about the world of trading? Keep reading to see if you have what it takes to be a barterer.

## A Real-Life Bartering Experience

At the end of every farmers' market, vendors often throw out foods that didn't sell, so in 2008, a Seattle farmers' market teamed up with a food bank called Northwest Harvest. The food bank set up a table at the market, and when the vendors brought their unsold veggies and fruits at the end of the day, the food bank packed it up and brought it to people who wouldn't have had food otherwise. It was a win-win situation. The farmers' market vendors didn't have to throw away unsold produce, and the food bank received fresh fruits and veggies for those in need.

## How to Barter

Already got some skills to trade? You might make out pretty well at a barter fair. At a barter fair, you can bring something like homemade soap, and trade it for almost anything else the other attendees has brought to exchange. In the late 1970s, in a time of economic uncertainty due to inflation, barter fairs became very popular.

If there are no barter fairs in your town, you can still barter with your friends and neighbors. Start by taking an inventory of what you've got that others might need. Maybe you can paint well, bake cookies, fix computers...anything has trade value if you can deliver.

Next, think about what you'd like in return for your skills. Do you need a haircut? Do you need help moving? Figure out what you need, and then start asking around to see who might be trade partners.

If you haven't found anyone to barter with, don't worry. You can still use your bartering skills at the local thrift store to haggle a lower price for that one-of-a-kind lamp you've been eyeing, or even at the mall, where sales clerks sometimes have the authority to lower a price to make a sale. Or you could head to your local barter club, a group of people who meet regularly to trade wares or services.

If direct trade is what you want, try advertising what you want to get rid of in a local print or online newspaper. Be sure to state that you'll take whatever's offered in return. You'll likely get a lot of emails requesting more information about your item. Some people will offer goods in return, but most will offer services instead.

## A Word to the Wise

Almost anything can be bartered for, but you have to follow some rules or your barter might fail. First, think carefully about what you need or want and what you're offering. The two should be in balance. Second, be clear from the beginning what you'll accept in return for your goods or services. Third, if you make an agreement, stick to it. Trustworthiness is essential to successful bartering.

Instead of having to find someone who wants your produce and has clothing to trade, you can sell your produce for money and then use that money to buy clothing from someone else. This system allows you to trade with a much wider range of people and get exactly what you need without having to go through a long series of trades.

So, while it's possible to trade goods and services without currency, it's not always practical or efficient. Currency has its own drawbacks, like the potential for inflation and economic inequality, but it also allows us to trade more easily and efficiently than we could without it.

input.text_cot: If all the flowers disappeared, how would you pollinate plants? Let's think step by step.

output.text_basic:
If all the bees disappeared, how would crops be fertilized, or how would plants be spread around? While there may be solutions for some of these questions, the ecological imbalance that even a minor change such as losing one type of insect would cause is unfathomable.

Bees, butterflies, beetles, ants, and wasps are all essential for carrying out a process called pollination. This is where pollens are transported around a plant to either self-pollinate, or fertilize that plant with another that can cross-pollinate. Without these insects, plant life would be severely limited.

As of 2021, many of our insects have been deemed endangered or at the brink of extinction. The most common reason for this loss is habitat destruction, as development and modernization continue. Other contributing factors are climate change, pesticides and genetically modified organisms (GMO’s) which we use to fight pests, disease and weeds.

According to the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources, and their Red List of Threatened Species, nearly 40% of invertebrate pollinators studied, such as bees and butterflies, face extinction globally. Of the bee population alone, a full third of all species are in this category. The loss of these insects will have a dire impact on the environment, agriculture and our food supply.

It is estimated that 75% of the world’s flowering plants rely on these pollinators. That number increases to more than 80% for our wild plants, and more than 35% of all globally produced foods, including nuts, fruits and vegetables. Insects also play a major role in the food chain with a variety of animals and birds feeding on them, providing pest control and pollutant control among other benefits.

While there are many things that can be done, one step that you can take is to create pollinator-friendly habitats. This can be done in your backyard or on your apartment balcony, and it can be incorporated into community spaces such as parks or green spaces.

The simplest way to help these creatures is by creating a pollinator garden. This involves providing sources of food (plants), water, cover and places to nest and reproduce. You can start with basic wildflowers that are native to your area and you can then plant various trees, fruiting and flowering shrubs. These not only provide cover, but also attract insects and birds who will also nest and carry out pollination.

Pollinator plants should bloom from early spring through fall. Most bees are generalist feeders and collect nectar and pollen from a variety of flowers. Some are specialists, and need specific types of plants while others, like butterflies, prefer clusters of brightly colored flowers.

Bees and other insects require water for hydration, but they also need a place to safely land. They do not like to sit on the edge of a container of water. A shallow container with a few rocks strategically placed in it allows the insects to have easy access to the water without accidentally drowning. This can be refreshed on a regular basis.

Another way to assist is by stopping the use of chemicals whenever possible on your property, both on your plants, and on the lawn. Pesticides and herbicides are indiscriminate; if they kill the weeds, or the insects you do not want, they will kill the ones you do want as well including butterflies, bees and other insects.

Weeds often provide food for the insects, and they also attract additional nectar and pollen sources. This is especially important early and late in the season when there may not be other plants available.

Avoid using GMO plants and seeds as these cross-pollinate with non-GMO plants and can alter the genetic make-up of native plant populations, thus reducing genetic diversity. Limiting the use of mulch is also important for native insects as they prefer more natural habitats where other insects and plants can thrive.

Mason bees are an excellent alternative to honeybees. They are solitary, so they do not produce honey, but they do carry out pollination. Each female lays her own eggs, typically in hollow stems or the holes in wood left by insects. You can create a mason bee house in a number of ways such as providing a board with drilled holes, or creating a container to hold tubes that contain the nesting materials. Insect hotels are also a great way to encourage bees, butterflies and other insects to nest. You can add these to your outdoor space or even inside if you have a light filled window.

You can go online to find a wealth of information to help you start your own pollinator garden and create habitats that are safe for bees, butterflies and a variety of other pollinating insects.

While there will still be pollination carried out by the wind, gravity and animals, the loss of this one category of insects could be devastating to the world. Plant life could be reduced, or altered, and agriculture would be affected. The ripple effects would be far reaching

We all have a part in this and by taking simple steps like these, you can help ensure that we continue to see these creatures for generations to come.

3. **Manual Pollination**: In the absence of pollinators, we could manually transfer pollen using tools like paintbrushes or cotton swabs. However, this would be extremely labor-intensive and impractical for large-scale farming.

5. **Water Pollination**: Certain aquatic plants use water to disperse their pollen. While not common, it's another alternative to animal-pollinated systems.

6. **Breeding for Self-Pollination**: Plant breeders could develop new varieties of plants that are capable of self-pollination. This would eliminate the need for external pollinators.

7. **Use of Robotic Pollinators**: In a futuristic scenario, robotic pollinators could be developed to mimic the role of bees and other pollinators. These could be programmed to visit flowers and transfer pollen.

Remember, the disappearance of all flowers would have catastrophic effects on ecosystems worldwide, far beyond just pollination issues. It's essential to protect our environment and preserve biodiversity.

If there were no more weekends, how would you plan your week and rests? Here is a personal story I wrote to remind myself and let you all know that life is too short to wait.

When I was twenty-two, I had a dream to see the sunset of the Himalayas. I started reading about the Himalayas every day. I read about the geography, weather, life, culture, cuisine, history, and mythology of the mountains. My search turned into obsession, and it came to a point when people started getting irritated. They used to comment, “Ankit, will you ever start talking about something else? You should come back to reality. You are stuck in dreaming about sunsets and snow.”

I am sure that we all have read or heard about the importance of being in the present and enjoying the current moment. You probably have heard some form of advice or philosophy such as:

“The greatest step towards a life of simplicity is to learn to let go.” ~ Steve Maraboli

“Sell your cleverness and buy bewilderment.” ~ Rumi

“There are two ways to live. You can live as if nothing is a miracle; you can live as if everything is a miracle.” ~ Albert Einstein

One day, out of irritation, a friend of mine quoted the famous line from Confucius, “Life is very short, and there’s no time for fussing and fighting, my friend.”

I had never given much attention to that quote; that day, it stopped and got etched in my memory. It brought a tear in my eyes, and for a brief moment, I got distracted from the beauty of the Himalayas. That day I truly understood that I should stop wasting my energy on the negativity.

Life is indeed beautiful, but in reality, we are so stuck in daily routines, work, and other activities that we forget what we truly love. We get so caught up with the negativities of life that we can’t appreciate or enjoy life’s gifts, nor do we see the beauty around us. Just like that day when a friend irritated me with the quote, and just like that, I realized:

Life is too short to wait. I can’t wait until Monday to start my healthy diet. I can’t wait until my next paycheck to buy that book or coursework I want. If I really want to eat that pizza, I should have it now. I can’t wait until I retire or for one day when I have time to take a long walk in the forest and listen to the rustling leaves or meditate near a cascading waterfall.

The fact is, there is no one-day waiting for anything; today is your one day. Stop waiting for time off or weekends, use your minutes and hours wisely. Life is too short to wait until we have more savings so that we can take that trip we want. If you think you can put things off for next year, stop. Life is too short to wait.

So I left my job, packed a small backpack, and trekked toward the foot of the Great Himalayas. I saw the most beautiful sunsets. I met the locals. I learned the local dialect. I learned their stories. I learned about their culture, traditions, the reasons they have to celebrate, and the way they live.

After four days on foot, I reached a small Himalayan settlement. It was surrounded by the mountains covered in clouds. I will never forget how beautiful that sight—the sunset over the white peaks—was. I had tears in my eyes. I was overwhelmed, to the point that I couldn’t speak. Even today, when I close my eyes, I can go back and see that scene.

So I urge you to take time to think about what you love. Maybe you would like to go and watch a beautiful sunrise or sunset on the beach. Maybe you would like to climb a mountain, learn a new skill, or simply spend more time with your family. Maybe you would like to travel, write that book you have always wanted to write, or simply take a long, leisurely walk. Find out what you want and go do it, because life is too short to wait.

If you enjoyed this post, please like it and share it! If you have any thoughts or questions, please leave them in the comments below.

Love,

Ankit

First, would you like to move to a place with a suitable climate? Why should you if you could live in your garden without the four-season system but with a suitable microclimate system instead?

## How to create a microclimate?

The microclimate is the climate of a small defined area that differs from the area around it. There are natural and artificial microclimates. For example, we are usually surrounded by an urban microclimate in the city.

To create a suitable microclimate in your garden, you need plants that can support the temperature you need for growing year-round. To make the garden even more comfortable, you can put up an awning or a tent and use energy-efficient light sources such as LED grow lamps, which help in the event of poor sunlight.

The microclimate can be changed by covering open spaces, protecting from wind currents, creating a barrier made of green walls, and using water features that naturally produce cooler temperatures.

## Microclimate zones according to temperature

Microclimates can vary according to the differences in temperature, which can significantly impact your plants. To create an all-season garden, you must therefore know the microclimate zones based on temperature:

Zone 1: 40° Fahrenheit (-5° Celsius)

It is a cold climate all year round. In this climatic zone, you can grow a limited number of plants that can withstand cold temperatures.

Zone 2: 50° Fahrenheit (10° Celsius)

This microclimate zone makes it possible to grow plants that prefer cool temperatures of around 50° Fahrenheit.

Zone 3: 65° Fahrenheit (18° Celsius)

You've reached a microclimate range where only the most temperature-resistant plants can grow. It is a temperate environment where low temperatures are almost constant.

Zone 4: 75° Fahrenheit (24° Celsius)

This temperature range is close to the optimal temperature for growing crops. It is the zone in the garden where indoor plants can be placed because it is not excessively hot nor excessively cool, especially if it is a shaded area.

Zone 5: 85° Fahrenheit (30° Celsius)

The last microclimate zone, with temperature ranges of up to 85° Fahrenheit, is suitable for plants that love the heat.

To make a microclimate in a small garden in an apartment, the trick is to make a microclimate system using the right accessories. By having LED grow lights for 24/7 light, an air ventilation system, a heat barrier, and an efficient watering system, you can create a small oasis in your urban garden, which would not be affected by external climatic events.

By combining microclimate zones, you can create the perfect garden and grow your plants, vegetables, or flowers any time of the year.

## Garden without seasons: plants to grow

After creating a perfect microclimate, you must select suitable plants for your garden. Here are some examples of plants that love various seasons:

### Winter plants

Winter plants are those that resist low temperatures. Examples are winter cabbages and leeks. Winter vegetables such as carrots and potatoes can be planted in February and harvested as late as May.

### Summer plants

Summer is the perfect season for growing most fruit and vegetables, such as tomatoes, peppers, and eggplants. This season is also favorable for growing aromatic herbs like mint, basil, thyme, and rosemary. Don't forget the classic summer plants like geraniums, begonias, and tulips.

### Autumn plants

Autumn is the time when you can grow and harvest leafy plants like lettuce, spinach, broccoli, and radishes. It's the best season for growing squash and root vegetables like carrots and potatoes.

### Spring plants

In the springtime, you can grow a wide variety of fruits and vegetables. Favorites are radishes, lettuces, cucumbers, tomatoes, and sweet and red peppers.

You can also grow fruit, such as kiwis, berries, and cherries, during the whole year with a proper microclimate system in your garden.

You can find the best way to make a microclimate system by shopping our indoor and outdoor grow light collections with their accessories like tents and grow bags. ## How to create a microclimate?

The microclimate is the climate of a small defined area that differs from the area around it. There are natural and artificial microclimates. For example, we are usually surrounded by an urban microclimate in the city.

To create a suitable microclimate in your garden, you need plants that can support the temperature you need for growing year-round. To make the garden even more comfortable, you can put up an awning or a tent and use energy-efficient light sources such as LED grow lamps, which help in the event of poor sunlight.

The microclimate can be changed by covering open spaces, protecting from wind currents, creating a barrier made of green walls, and using water features that naturally produce cooler temperatures.

## Microclimate zones according to temperature

Microclimates can vary according to the differences in temperature, which can significantly impact your plants. To create an all-season garden, you must therefore know the microclimate zones based on temperature:

Zone 1: 40° Fahrenheit (-5° Celsius)

It is a cold climate all year round. In this climatic zone, you can grow a limited number of plants that can withstand cold temperatures.

Zone 2: 50° Fahrenheit (10° Celsius)

This microclimate zone makes it possible to grow plants that prefer cool temperatures of around 50° Fahrenheit.

Zone 3: 65° Fahrenheit (18° Celsius)

You've reached a microclimate range where only the most temperature-resistant plants can grow. It is a temperate environment where low temperatures are almost constant.

Zone 4: 75° Fahrenheit (24° Celsius)

This temperature range is close to the optimal temperature for growing crops. It is the zone in the garden where indoor plants can be placed because it is not excessively hot nor excessively cool, especially if it is a shaded area.

Zone 5: 85° Fahrenheit (30° Celsius)

The last microclimate zone, with temperature ranges of up to 85° Fahrenheit, is suitable for plants that love the heat.

To make a microclimate in a small garden in an apartment, the trick is to make a microclimate system using the right accessories. By having LED grow lights for 24/7 light, an air ventilation system, a heat barrier, and an efficient watering system, you can create a small oasis in your urban garden, which would not be affected by external climatic events.

By combining microclimate zones, you can create the perfect garden and grow your plants, vegetables, or flowers any time of the year.

## Garden without seasons: plants to grow

After creating a perfect microclimate, you must select suitable plants for your garden. Here are some examples of plants that love various seasons:

### Winter plants

Winter plants are those that resist low temperatures. Examples are winter cabbages and leeks. Winter vegetables such as carrots and potatoes can be planted in February and harvested as late as May.

### Summer plants

Summer is the perfect season for growing most fruit and vegetables, such as tomatoes, peppers, and eggplants. This season is also favorable for growing aromatic herbs like mint, basil, thyme, and rosemary. Don't forget the classic summer plants like geraniums, begonias, and tulips.

### Autumn plants

Autumn is the time when you can grow and harvest leafy plants like lettuce, spinach, broccoli, and radishes. It's the best season for growing squash and root vegetables like carrots and potatoes.

### Spring plants

In the springtime, you can grow a wide variety of fruits and vegetables. Favorites are radishes, lettuces, cucumbers, tomatoes, and sweet and red peppers.

You can also grow fruit, such as kiwis, berries, and cherries, during the whole year with a proper microclimate system in your garden.

You can find the best way to make a microclimate system by shopping our indoor and outdoor grow light collections with their accessories like tents and grow bags.
