These are a few of the questions Mary Ellen Matthews, a volunteer with the ALS Association Wisconsin Chapter, says she had to think about while helping her uncle, Dave, live with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Matthews says even though it’s been 15 years since her uncle passed away from the disease, she still thinks about him and his struggles often.

ALS, also called Lou Gehrig’s disease, is a fatal motor neuron disease with no known cause and no cure. According to the ALS Association, approximately 6,400 people in the United States are diagnosed each year with ALS, while more than 200,000 Americans may be living with the disease at any given time.

With ALS, nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord gradually break down and die, which prevents the brain from signaling the muscles to move. Eventually, people with ALS lose the ability to initiate and control muscle movement, which leads to total paralysis and death, usually within two to five years after diagnosis.

Even with such a prognosis, Matthews says her family refused to let despair seep in. Instead, they came together to creatively make everyday tasks possible even as the disease progressed.

For example, Matthews says when her uncle could no longer lift his arms, relatives and friends fashioned special utensils, such as a fork with a large, ergonomic handle, so he could feed himself. Then, when Dave could no longer get out of bed, they devised a sling he could use to pull himself up to a seated position.

“Everybody rallied around him, and we would have ‘invention nights,’ where my uncle would say, ‘I need this.’ We would go down in the basement and try to make it for him,” Matthews says.

Even daily hygiene tasks, such as brushing one’s teeth, were still possible with the help of family. They outfitted an electric toothbrush with a suction cup and attached it to his mattress so he could brush his teeth in the morning by pushing it away with his feet.

“Little things like that, he’d figure out, and he didn’t want people to feel sorry for him,” Matthews says. “People would say, ‘Why do you do that yourself?’ And he said, ‘If I didn’t, what would be there for me?’ I can’t tell you how many people were just in awe of him and how he handled things.”

At the time, Matthews was a young married mother, working and raising her family in Marshfield. While she had volunteered in her local community, she had never volunteered with an organization like the ALS Association. However, Matthews says she knew she wanted to help people who also were going through what her uncle had experienced.

“[After my uncle died,] people were still dying. I knew in my heart I wanted to be able to help those who were dying in that way,” Matthews says.

Thus, she contacted the ALS Association Wisconsin Chapter in 2003. Since then, she has volunteered thousands of hours for various events and support groups in her region.

In 2014, she became the first regional leader of the Wausau ALS Support Group and has helped transform the group from a small gathering of three families at the local hospital to a large group of nearly 30 families at a new location, the YMCA in Weston.

Matthews recalls that in the first three years of leading the group, it only met once because of low attendance. She decided to research support groups from around the nation to see how she could improve the local group.

After visiting other support groups and taking note of their organization and structure, Matthews came up with a plan to improve the Wausau ALS Support Group. She decided to hold smaller, roundtable discussions and change the location to the YMCA, which offers more space for growth and expansion. The group typically meets the last Monday of each month.

Now, Matthews says the group attracts families from places like Stevens Point and Rhinelander, as well as Marshfield.

“I just had a lady tell me at the last meeting, ‘You are amazing, Mary Ellen, and thank you for providing something that is so wonderful. It’s nice to have my family hear from others who are going through this. I’ve said this to you before, but you are amazing, and this group has grown so huge. How do you do it?’ And I didn’t want to tell her that was part of the reason for changing the group: I kind of want to grow it,” Matthews says.

She also has found other ways to grow her volunteerism. After retiring from her part-time job at the Wausau Area Chamber of Commerce, she began volunteering at WSAW-TV and WJFW-TV. At WSAW, her main responsibilities are to provide video segments for the morning and noon news.

“It’s a lot of fun. It’s a completely different world to me, so that’s why I started volunteering there,” Matthews says.

For the past two years, she has volunteered for “ALS Days” held at the news stations in March. The “ALS Days” are opportunities for a few patients living with ALS and their families to attend the news station for a day and share their stories on television. Matthews says she enjoys making these experiences possible for her clients with ALS.

One time, she volunteered with a mother who brought her young daughter to the news station with her. Matthews says it is moments like this one that are incredibly memorable.

“They came in on a Sunday, and that little girl just had a blast. She got to pretend she was a weather reporter, so she had a blast. It was fun, you know, and it’s not often they get to see that,” Matthews says.

In addition to finding ways to support people living with ALS, Matthews also has been able to honor the legacy of her uncle through her volunteer work with the organization. For example, she started an ALS Walk Team, the Sluggers, to raise money for the ALS Association. According to its website, her team has raised more than $64,000 for the ALS Association so far, with the goal of raising $100,000 by 2020.

In 2016, she received the Golden Heart Award for her volunteerism from the ALS Association Midwest Chapter and was recognized a second time this year for her efforts. She also was featured in the ALS Association 2017 annual report.

Matthews’ colleague and support group member Kimberly Grosche said in the report that Matthews’ “work touches every patient in our service area and has created a community of support and love that is unmatched.”

This love is most evident in how Matthews connects with everyone she meets living with ALS. In fact, she has become friendly with a woman who lives in the same town as she does.

A few years ago, Matthews befriended the woman after her husband, who had ALS, passed away. At the time, the woman did not attend the ALS Support Group in Wausau, so Matthews made a special effort to befriend her and bring her into the group’s fold.

Matthews says the woman has benefited from learning from other group members.

“She’s gone to some of the meetings and said, ‘I’m so glad I joined or I wouldn’t have known this or that,’” Matthews says.

Beyond making meaningful connections with ALS patients and their families, Matthews also enjoys volunteering in general because of the feeling of fulfillment that accompanies it. She has been volunteering in her community for so long that it has become a part of her character.

“You just have this feeling of satisfaction and fulfillment because we can all give. Anybody can do it in any way. Whether it’s an hour a month, an hour a week, or a couple hours a week, you definitely get that good feeling inside,” Matthews says.

And for her clients with ALS, knowing that someone like Matthews has their best interests at heart makes all the difference.

“In this journey, you encounter people, like Mary Ellen, who have the biggest hearts and are the most committed. They are the rare people who just want to make a difference in people’s lives,” Grosche said in the ALS Association 2017 annual report.

Matthews believes she can make a difference in other people’s lives by showing them love and compassion. A big part of that love is showing people who are living with ALS that they are not alone.

“When I say I understand, I think it is important for them to know I understand because I’ve been there and seen what my uncle has gone through. I’m not sure many people can say they understand, and I think that gives them a little bit of reassurance: ‘You know what? She does understand, and she cares,’” Matthews says.

For more information about the Wausau ALS Support Group, contact the ALS Association Wisconsin Chapter at 888-949-2577 or [email protected]; or visit the Wisconsin Chapter’s website at wis.alsa.org and click on the Find Support tab. The ALS Association Wisconsin Chapter is located at N57 W13565 Silver Spring Dr., Menomonee Falls.

More Information

- The ALS Association: alsa.org
- ALS Association Wisconsin Chapter: alsa.org/chapters/wi/
- Wausau ALS Support Group: alsa.org/news-events/events/wlc/wausau-als-support-group/

- You could crawl.
- You could use a skateboard.
- You could drive a car.
- You could ride a bike.
- You could ride a horse.

If you're an engineer, you can improve on the bike. Rather than having pedals and a chain that move a rear wheel, you can make the bike use the motion of your arms. After all, in many sports, your legs do very little while you're making quick movements with your arms. Think about skiing, swimming and rowing — your legs are there for balance, but your arms do most of the work. Perhaps an arm-powered bicycle, or "armcycle," would be useful for disabled people.

During research for such a device, it turns out someone had indeed invented a type of armcycle before [source: Stemler]. The next question, of course, is can you ride it? While I didn't have access to an actual armcycle, I made one using an exercise machine made for strengthening the arms. The motion was similar.

While I can't say it was easy to ride, it was definitely possible. I moved slowly and managed to gain enough momentum to keep making progress. The exercise machine provided a smooth ride, unlike a regular bike that can jostle about, so I was fairly comfortable. If such a machine could be modified to have brakes to help control speed and to steer, it could provide a fun and alternative means of transportation for people who can't use their legs. In fact, I rode this contraption through my local grocery store to show the possibilities. My fellow shoppers didn't seem that surprised at all. I think they were just happy not to have to listen to the whirring of the typical motorized wheelchair.

### Author's Note: Will an arm-powered bike work?

I always wonder if people will be offended by a question like, "What if you can no longer stand up?" Some people may feel like I'm suggesting they are going to be injured or disabled. Of course, that's never my intent. I'm just trying to get people to think: "What if I couldn't use my arms? What if I couldn't use my legs? What if I couldn't see? What if I couldn't hear?" Such questions can lead to some pretty cool inventions.

### Sources

- BikeHacks.com. "Flexible Arms for a Smooth and Safe Front Handlebar Ride." (Jan. 16, 2013) http://bikehacks.com/bikehacks/2011/04/flexible-arms-for-a-smooth-and-safe-front-handlebar-ride.html
- The Great Bicycle Experiment. "Bicycle History." (Jan. 16, 2013) http://www.bikexprt.com/bicycle/
- Stemler, Bruce. "Recumbent and other arm-powered bikes allow hands-free leg operation." American College of Sports Medicine. Nov. 15, 2010. (Jan. 16, 2013) http://www.acsm.org/access-to-jacm/recumbent-and-other-arm-powered-bikes-allow-hands-free-leg-operation
- Vesco, Frank. "How to pedal a bike with your arms." Yanko Design. Feb. 8, 2008. (Jan. 16, 2013) http://www.yankodesign.com/2008/02/08/how-to-pedal-a-bike-with-your-arms/

If you're an engineer, you can improve on the bike. Rather than having pedals and a chain that move a rear wheel, you can make the bike use the motion of your arms. After all, in many sports, your legs do very little while you're making quick movements with your arms. Think about skiing, swimming and rowing — your legs are there for balance, but your arms do most of the work. Perhaps an arm-powered bicycle, or "armcycle," would be useful for disabled people.

During research for such a device, it turns out someone had indeed invented a type of armcycle before [source: Stemler]. The next question, of course, is can you ride it? While I didn't have access to an actual armcycle, I made one using an exercise machine made for strengthening the arms. The motion was similar.

While I can't say it was easy to ride, it was definitely possible. I moved slowly and managed to gain enough momentum to keep making progress. The exercise machine provided a smooth ride, unlike a regular bike that can jostle about, so I was fairly comfortable. If such a machine could be modified to have brakes to help control speed and to steer, it could provide a fun and alternative means of transportation for people who can't use their legs. In fact, I rode this contraption through my local grocery store to show the possibilities. My fellow shoppers didn't seem that surprised at all. I think they were just happy not to have to listen to the whirring of the typical motorized wheelchair.

Of course, that's never my intent. I'm just trying to get people to think: "What if I couldn't use my arms? What if I couldn't use my legs? What if I couldn't see? What if I couldn't hear?" Such questions can lead to some pretty cool inventions.

input.text_cot: If all digital data were lost, how would you store information? Let's think step by step.

output.text_basic:
There are several physical forms that can endure for long periods of time:

1. Paper: While acidic paper breaks down much too quickly, alkaline paper can last for hundreds of years. However, acidic paper has been the norm for much of history, so even old tomes may not last beyond the 21st century.
2. Stone: A granite slab with an engraving can last for tens of thousands, or even millions of years, as long as it doesn't suffer catastrophic damage.
3. DNA: DNA is incredibly efficient, requiring less than a nanogram of volume for every letter in a trillion-letter code. DNA and RNA have survived for at least 40 million years, and may have survived for centuries of millions.

Of these three, only DNA is dense enough to hold all of the world's information at once. But how could it be done?

Well, there are 10^24 bytes in total human knowledge. Since there are 3 billion bps (base pairs) in a human genome, you would need 3 * 10^17 human genomes of information.

The human body can create a few trillion new cells each day. Given these facts, you could create new DNA to store all of human knowledge every eight-tenths of a second, or 37 times every minute. Or, you could generate 20 terabytes of storage a day on a human body.

As long as this DNA wasn't contaminated, or mixed up with the other DNA in the body, it could last for millions of years. And when it comes time to retrieve the information, we could always grow and destroy cells containing encoded data, with nothing but the original genome remaining.

A company called Cambrian Genomics wants to sell genomes on demand. At present, that's not entirely possible, since the tools to cheaply create and edit genes are still being developed, but the company promises to do whatever is possible for its customers, including creating new plant species or even writing messages in someone's genome (presumably without harming them).

So whether through Cambrian or something similar, we may one day be able to buy customizable, long-term DNA storage and do so in very large quantities.

output.text_cot:
The easiest solution would be books, however, keeping a book safe from external factors like fire, water and other physical damage is a difficult task. The next best option would be etching the information on an unyielding medium. This could be stone or engraved metals, however, they would be difficult to transport.

What if we found a way to combine both of these aspects? A metal book that is lightweight, small and able to withstand extreme conditions. This solution could even help us to expand our knowledge of space and explore the universe outside our world.

This is exactly the idea behind the Rosetta Disk.

#### THE ELEMENTS OF THE ROSSETTA DISK

The Rosetta Disk is:
- A micro-etched nickel disk 3 inches in diameter and 0.1 inches thick
- The surface of its backside contains 13,000 pages of information micro-etched in unalterable platinum
- The mini-disk weighs about half an ounce
- The pages on the disk are displayed in 500 languages, 12 scripts and 28 styles. In the center are English and the top 10 languages, followed by other common languages organized by regional popularity.
- The outer rim depicts the story of the creation of the Rosetta Disk. In all, there are 1,500 images on the disk

The most impressive aspect of the Rosetta Disk is its small size. The device can easily fit in the palm of a hand, yet contains an enormous amount of knowledge on the surface of its tiny 3-inch size.

The Rosetta Disk is so small that you could easily fit four of them in an envelope or even keep one in a wallet.

#### HOW TO ACCESS THE INFORMATION?

To read the text on the disk it requires a computer controlled microscope to translate the small images into a digital format, which is then read as text. 

The Rosetta Disk is an example of near-permanent, dense data storage. If you were to engrave the text of a book on this disk's surface, the text would last billions of years - even if the solar system were to undergo a cataclysmic event.

It's not hard to understand why the Rosetta Disk is such an impressive achievement. As long as humans continue to innovate, these types of devices could prove critical for storing and preserving knowledge in the case of a disaster that threatens the very existence of mankind and the civilization that we have so painstakingly created.

#### WHERE CAN I FIND AND SEE THE ONE REAL ROSSETTA DISK?

The one true Rosetta Disk exists currently in a secure location in the US. The disk has been exhibited in numerous museums and libraries around the world as a part of the permanent collection or as a special exhibit.

A list of these locations can be found at: http://rosettaproject.org/participate/visit/

#### ABOUT THE PROJECT

The Rosetta Project at The Long Now Foundation was co-founded by computer scientist and entrepreneur, Dr. Brewster Kahle in 2003. The Long Now Foundation is dedicated to developing long-term thinking and infrastructure to improve the sustainability of our civilization.

The Rosetta Project is designed to save and share the world's language knowledge and reduce language loss. The project was inspired by the original Rosetta Stone, which was discovered in 1799 in Rosetta, Egypt. The stone slab contains inscriptions in three scripts using three different languages: Egyptian hieroglyphs, Demotic script, and Ancient Greek. By comparing these translations, linguists were able decipher the hieroglyphs, leading to an increased understanding of the ancient Egyptian empire.

The Rosetta Project uses technology to preserve all the world's written languages before they potentially disappear. The Rosetta Disk contains the top 1,500 most frequently used words from over 1,000 world languages. The disk also contains 500 pages of text from a variety of works in 500 languages. The goal is to create a dense, long-term archive of language that can help to preserve all living languages.

The Rosetta Project website includes a library of over 100,000 digital pages of information in 2,500 languages.

#### ROSSETTA DISK IN POP CULTURE

If you like a good story (especially during these times of limited social activities), the Rosetta Disk has featured in both the video game and television show "The Expanse." The Rosetta Disk in "The Expanse" contains the full genetic code for human beings. The show is based on a series of novels by Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck (writing as James S.A. Corey). A similar concept of genetic data storage is also used in the book "The Martian" by Andy Weir.

#### WHAT CAN I DO NOW?

The concept of storing information is not only important for preserving human history, but it also plays a role in every aspect of our daily lives. Our computers, phones, smart watches, and televisions all store information in some way or another. This gives us the ability to interact with our world in ways that previously did not exist.

There is a huge amount of information available on the internet. If you want to expand your knowledge, you can access a vast amount of information from the comfort of your own home.

1. Browse:

Browse around different websites to expand your understanding of a specific topic or for a general interest.

- Academia.edu

2. Explore:

- Yahoo
- Bing

- StartPage

- Qwant

3. Experience:

Expanding your knowledge is not limited to learning facts or theory alone.

The internet also allows us to interact with people from all over the world and to experience different cultures. You could:

- Watch a movie
- Listen to music
- Play games
- Browse art
- Take a virtual tour
- Watch performances
- Listen to speeches
- Chat or talk to people

The power of the internet can be harnessed to explore almost every single topic you could think of. So, go ahead and let your curiosity run free!

If you want, you can even check on the latest Covid-19 information from around the world.

Question: If all digital data were lost, how would you store information? Let's think step by step.
Answer: 
The easiest solution would be books, however, keeping a book safe from external factors like fire, water and other physical damage is a difficult task. The next best option would be etching the information on an unyielding medium. This could be stone or engraved metals, however, they would be difficult to transport.

What if we found a way to combine both of these aspects? A metal book that is lightweight, small and able to withstand extreme conditions. This solution could even help us to expand our knowledge of space and explore the universe outside our world.

This is exactly the idea behind the Rosetta Disk.

#### THE ELEMENTS OF THE ROSSETTA DISK

The Rosetta Disk is:
- A micro-etched nickel disk 3 inches in diameter and 0.1 inches thick
- The surface of its backside contains 13,000 pages of information micro-etched in unalterable platinum
- The mini-disk weighs about half an ounce
- The pages on the disk are displayed in 500 languages, 12 scripts and 28 styles. In the center are English and the top 10 languages, followed by other common languages organized by regional popularity.
- The outer rim depicts the story of the creation of the Rosetta Disk. In all, there are 1,500 images on the disk

The most impressive aspect of the Rosetta Disk is its small size. The device can easily fit in the palm of a hand, yet contains an enormous amount of knowledge on the surface of its tiny 3-inch size.

The Rosetta Disk is so small that you could easily fit four of them in an envelope or even keep one in a wallet.

#### HOW TO ACCESS THE INFORMATION?

To read the text on the disk it requires a computer controlled microscope to translate the small images into a digital format, which is then read as text. 

The Rosetta Disk is an example of near-permanent, dense data storage. If you were to engrave the text of a book on this disk's surface, the text would last billions of years - even if the solar system were to undergo a cataclysmic event.

It's not hard to understand why the Rosetta Disk is such an impressive achievement. As long as humans continue to innovate, these types of devices could prove critical for storing and preserving knowledge in the case of a disaster that threatens the very existence of mankind and the civilization that we have so painstakingly created.

#### WHERE CAN I FIND AND SEE THE ONE REAL ROSSETTA DISK?

The one true Rosetta Disk exists currently in a secure location in the US. The disk has been exhibited in numerous museums and libraries around the world as a part of the permanent collection or as a special exhibit.

A list of these locations can be found at: http://rosettaproject.org/participate/visit/

#### ABOUT THE PROJECT

The Rosetta Project at The Long Now Foundation was co-founded by computer scientist and entrepreneur, Dr. Brewster Kahle in 2003. The Long Now Foundation is dedicated to developing long-term thinking and infrastructure to improve the sustainability of our civilization.

The Rosetta Project is designed to save and share the world's language knowledge and reduce language loss. The project was inspired by the original Rosetta Stone, which was discovered in 1799 in Rosetta, Egypt. The stone slab contains inscriptions in three scripts using three different languages: Egyptian hieroglyphs, Demotic script, and Ancient Greek. By comparing these translations, linguists were able decipher the hieroglyphs, leading to an increased understanding of the ancient Egyptian empire.

The Rosetta Project uses technology to preserve all the world's written languages before they potentially disappear. The Rosetta Disk contains the top 1,500 most frequently used words from over 1,000 world languages. The disk also contains 500 pages of text from a variety of works in 500 languages. The goal is to create a dense, long-term archive of language that can help to preserve all living languages.

The Rosetta Project website includes a library of over 100,000 digital pages of information in 2,500 languages.

#### ROSSETTA DISK IN POP CULTURE

If you like a good story (especially during these times of limited social activities), the Rosetta Disk has featured in both the video game and television show "The Expanse." The Rosetta Disk in "The Expanse" contains the full genetic code for human beings. The show is based on a series of novels by Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck (writing as James S.A. Corey). A similar concept of genetic data storage is also used in the book "The Martian" by Andy Weir.

The concept of storing information is not only important for preserving human history, but it also plays a role in every aspect of our daily lives. Our computers, phones, smart watches, and televisions all store information in some way or another. This gives us the ability to interact with our world in ways that previously did not exist.

You'd be in quite a pickle without any blades at your disposal, so it's a good thing that this handy invention known as the paper cutter exists. Sure, it might just be a piece of metal with a handle, but it makes the act of shearing through something so much easier. Plus, when you really think about it, paper cutters are really just big, long knives, so you still have the satisfaction of manually cutting things without accidentally cutting yourself. If you work in an office or any type of field where the handling of paper is common, buying a paper cutter would be a wise investment. And luckily for you, we've got all the information you need in order to buy a paper cutter that best suits your situation.

## What is a paper cutter?

Just because you can tear a piece of paper in two doesn't mean it's easy—or even attractive looking. Using a paper cutter is the most hassle-free and precise way to cut down a large stack or to cut paper down to a specific size. The term "paper cutter" can be used for both manual and electric guillotine cutters. These come in a variety of sizes, depending on your needs and the amount of counter space you have to spare.

The most rudimentary paper cutter you can buy has a long, sharp blade that is affixed vertically and rests under a long piece of metal that guards your fingers from accidents. More advanced models have adjustable depth stops and a table that tilts, so you can use it as an angled cutting board, too. However, there is a difference between paper cutters and paper trimmers. Trimmers are typically designed for everyday use, are smaller, and have an integrated ruler for quick and easy measurement of where to cut.

Most paper cutters are made with metal blades, but some feature a rotary blade, which is common for models suitable for thicker cardstock. Electric guillotines (also known as cutting machines) are best for high-capacity users, and they usually employ a rotary cutter, which glides up and down a track with the help of a motor. They can also feature angled blades, so you can create creases and clean edges on documents without completely cutting them through.

## Who needs a paper cutter?

Anyone who ever has to cut paper can benefit from the precision a paper cutter offers. This also includes the cutting of cardboard, plastic, and foam core. For heavy-duty cutting, electric cutters allow for faster continuous cuts. But for basic needs, manual paper cutters are the most affordable and accessible.

Artists and design professionals can also benefit from the use of these machines, as they can cleanly prepare and resize prints or other materials in a flash. Additionally, paper cutters with multiple blades can help DIYers create precise collages and card stocks in no time.

People who work with delicate materials might prefer a rotary cutter—that is, a blade that rolls along the underside of a stationary piece of metal. This design is preferred for crafting and other similar uses, where delicate cutting is a must.

## How to choose the best paper cutter

Most desktop paper cutters are fairly similar, so the biggest considerations are whether or not you need an angled cutter for clean creasing, a built-in depth stop for consistency, and how thick your materials can be.

More advanced models that cater to those with more intense cutting needs are designed to allow for more efficient cutting of stacks of paper or other materials as well. If you're in a professional setting or you have a heavy-duty cutting job at hand, consider a machine with a motor.

For those interested in using their cutter for DIY work, consider rotary blades (which offer more precise cuts) or a guillotine cutter with several blades. These two options are the most beginner-friendly for intricate cutting jobs. For those with more experience, consider a paper cutter with additional features, such as a creaser bar.

## How much should you spend on a paper cutter?

Depending on the cutting capacity of the model you choose, paper cutters can range from $20 to $800. If you're only using your cutter on small DIY projects, expect to pay around $50 to $100 for a more durable option that suits your needs.

For everyday office use, you can expect to pay about $150 to $200 for more advanced models. For those in the arts and design fields, or those who need one for high-capacity use, you can expect to pay between $300 and $800.

## How we chose these paper cutters

To select the best paper cutters, we first looked at a few dozen options across all price ranges and then narrowed our list by looking at the specifications and reviews.

For DIY users, we looked for models that had either rotary blades or guillotine cutters with multiple blades. To ensure that these cutters were up to snuff, we scoured customer testimonials—specifically, those left on retailer websites—to gauge their durability, accuracy, and ease of use.

Because DIY users might expect to use their cutters more regularly, our focus was on finding a blend of affordability and functionality. So for smaller jobs, we steered clear of manual guillotines and toward rotary and multiple-blade models.

For regular office use, we focused more on affordability and the utility that users would need. Thus, we concentrated largely on basic guillotine cutters with simple depth stop adjuster.

In keeping with the need for high-capacity cutting, we leaned toward electric guillotines for the heavy-duty category. These cutters boast the best durability, accuracy, and consistency and can also accommodate thicker materials with ease.

In terms of functionality, all of the paper cutters we recommend have a clamping mechanism that ensures documents stay in place, adjustable guides, and the ability to lock in place so multiple sheets can be easily measured and cut. Additionally, all models have blade-protection guards.

As always, these picks represent what we think are the best options to fit most people's needs, so we'd love to hear about your personal experience in the comments below. Whether you want to share a favorite paper cutter or suggest another cutting machine you love, we look forward to hearing from you!

output.text_basic:
You should think about this problem, because scientists don’t expect all of our highways to survive climate change.

Global warming is causing the earth’s great ice sheets to melt, including the massive bodies of ice that cover Greenland and Antarctica. This is causing sea levels to rise, which is already causing trouble for people who live in coastal areas around the world.

If all those ice sheets melt entirely, sea levels will rise 230 feet (70 meters), scientists predict. This would wipe out nearly all of the Earth’s cities, and most roads would be covered by the sea.

So how would you travel through a world of entirely submerged roads, and no dry land left except mountaintops?

Here are a few options you could choose from, if such a world comes to be.

## 1. Hydrofoil boats

Hydrofoils are a type of watercraft where the hull lifts out of the water once the craft reaches a certain speed. Lifted out of the water, these vessels can move through the water the way a bird moves through the air, which could offer a faster and more convenient mode of transportation over long distances.

Hydrofoil boats could even reach the speed of cars and are less susceptible to sea conditions, such as waves and currents.

In short, hydrofoil boats are essentially airplanes that can travel on water, rather than through the sky.

## 2. Submarines

The human love of submarines actually predates the invention of automobiles. In 1829, the US Navy designed a submarine capable of submerging itself under water, but it was a failed project, as the vehicle was not designed to surface.

In the mid-1800s, a Swiss inventor and engineer named Wilhelm Bauer designed a submarine that could be propelled through water, like a ship at the surface, but could also submerge itself underwater to evade detection. That design went on to influence the design of modern submarines.

Subs move quietly underwater, making them almost undetectable without sonar. And unlike hydrofoil boats, subs do not require the water to remain calm.

Submarines might also be a good option for people who live on mountaintops, as subs could dock at underwater port cities near where they live.

## 3. Electric aircraft

If we learn how to overcome the current challenges, electric aircraft might be a great option for travelers in the distant future.

At the moment, electric aircraft are still at the experimental stage, with limited-range electric airplanes and quadcopter-type drones being the closest we have to commercially viable models. But once the technology develops, electric airplanes could potentially carry hundreds of passengers long distances without the need for refueling, as battery recharging technology develops from a nightly charging session to a 20-minute pause at a charging stand.

So, if all the roads are flooded and unpassable, electric airplanes would be an easy and convenient way to travel. But even if the climate doesn’t flood all the roads, it would be great if we could just fly off to our destinations anyway.

## 4. High-speed trains

If submarines, electric aircraft, and hydrofoil boats aren’t quite your style, there’s always high-speed trains. We already know they’re an awesome form of travel, with some trains in Japan capable of speeds as high as 375 mph (600 km/h).

High-speed trains would be a terrific way to go if you’re living on a mountaintop and want to travel long distances through the air rather than across the sea.

So while the melted ice sheets may leave us with few options to travel on dry land, these four types of transportation offer more ways to get around a world that looks a lot different than it does now.

Step 1: Identify the sources of water

Even without rain, there are still ways to collect water. Some possible sources include:

1. Dew: Collect dew from grass or plants using a clean cloth or sponge.
2. Groundwater: If you have access to a well or a natural spring, you can collect groundwater.
3. Rivers, streams, or lakes: If there are any bodies of water nearby, you can collect water from them. However, keep in mind that this water may need to be treated before consumption.
4. Condensation: You can create a simple solar still to collect condensation from the air.

Step 2: Collect the water

Once you've identified potential sources of water, you need to collect it. Here are some methods for collecting water from various sources:

1. Dew: Lay out a clean cloth or piece of plastic overnight to collect dew. In the morning, gather the cloth and wring out the water into a container.
2. Groundwater: Use a bucket or a pump to extract water from a well or natural spring. Make sure to keep the equipment clean to avoid contamination.
3. Rivers, streams, or lakes: Use a bucket, cup, or other container to scoop water from the source. If possible, try to filter the water through a clean cloth or coffee filter to remove debris and larger particles.
4. Condensation: Set up a solar still by digging a hole in the ground, placing a container in the center, and covering the hole with a clear plastic sheet. Secure the edges of the plastic with rocks or soil. As the sun heats the ground, moisture from the soil and air will condense on the plastic and drip into the container.

Step 3: Treat the water

Depending on the source of the water, it may need to be treated before consumption. Here are some methods for treating water:

1. Boiling: Bring the water to a rolling boil for at least one minute to kill bacteria and viruses.
2. Chemical treatment: Add water purification tablets or a few drops of unscented household bleach (5-6% sodium hypochlorite) to the water. Follow the instructions on the packaging or consult a reliable source for the correct dosage.
3. Filtration: Pass the water through a filter with a pore size of 0.1 microns or smaller to remove bacteria, protozoa, and some viruses.

Remember, it's essential to collect water from clean sources and treat it properly before consuming it to avoid illness.

For example, how would you know if a sharp knife was sliding toward your finger? How would you protect your finger from being cut?

Suppose you have two children, one is a 10-year-old boy and the other is a 12-year-old girl. They tell you they wish to marry each other. You are very upset and feel that they are too young to make such an important decision, so you refuse to give your blessing. They say that they love each other very much and that they intend to run away together to get married. Is this child abuse?

—D.G., North Hollywood

I've never heard of any law that defines parental prevention of child marriage as child abuse. There's no way I could give an opinion as to whether that could or should be the law.

But I can tell you what I think. While I can understand both the children's position and the parents', the children don't--and legally can't--have the right to marry. Until then, the question of whether this is child abuse by the parents would depend on the parents' reasons for refusing to give their blessing.

For example, if the 10-year-old boy wants to get married only to have a younger wife, I would think it is not child abuse by the parents to prevent that. On the other hand, if the young are in love, and their reasons for wanting to marry are not unreasonable, I would think that the parents would be unfairly hurting their children if they prevented them from doing so. Then again, since neither child is old enough to enter into a marriage, the question of whether it was child abuse might be moot.

On the other hand, it might be that the parents should agree to the marriage on the condition that the young couple agree that they are not bound by this marriage if they change their minds once they reach the age of majority.

•••

If I am in a public place such as a department store and am robbed on the premises, is the store or the management of the store responsible for the loss?

—W.L.

It would appear that you are asking if a department store or other commercial business establishment is liable for your losses if you suffer a theft while in their premises. Since the establishment generally has "no control" over the criminal conduct of a thief, unless the business itself was negligent in some manner in preventing or controlling access to the stolen property, a business would probably not be liable under normal circumstances.

•••

If a person is injured, and a close family member is the doctor, and for the sake of family peace, the doctor does not perform a necessary surgery, if the person dies as a result, is the doctor at risk of a law suit by the family member or the deceased's estate?

—O.C.S.

Yes. If a doctor has a patient who requires necessary medical treatment, and the doctor's reasons for not providing such treatment is only to avoid emotional family issues, then such behavior by the doctor would generally be totally inappropriate and inexcusable.

By choosing the path of refusing to treat a family member in order to avoid family issues, the doctor would be risking the health, well-being and indeed the very life of the family member. While a doctor cannot be held responsible for every failure of treatment, doctors certainly do not have the right to avoid performing medical procedures and endangering the very lives of a patient based simply on family issues.

In the event of a such a death, there probably would be a lawsuit based on medical malpractice, wrongful death, possibly battery and perhaps even elder abuse, depending on the circumstances.

You wouldn't be able to feel pain or pressure, so even cutting yourself or feeling a pinprick wouldn't be possible. You wouldn't feel any warmth or cold either, so you could burn yourself badly and never know it. It would be possible to break a bone and not discover it for years, since neither the pain of the injury Nor the swelling would be noticed. You would also have an increased likelihood of developing an infection from open wounds, but that danger would go unnoticed, since you wouldn't feel the pain or the increased warmth that often accompanies such a situation. Basically, you would be in constant danger of hurting yourself and not even knowing it until the damage were done.

That is how I would compare the state of my mind to that of not being able to feel physical sensation. Without any spiritual sensitivity to tune into, I have felt emotionally and spiritually distant from my surroundings much the same way as someone without the ability to feel physical sensation would be from the world. It's a lot like what I experienced when I first got back into the saddle of the horse, when my body couldn't feel anything due to the intense freezing of my muscles. That's how it has been, both emotionally and spiritually, for the past several months.

Before my break from social media, the time I spent on Facebook and Twitter was my main source of social interaction. That was what I used to maintain a connection to my community and the world. As I have progressed through physical therapy, however, I have been spending a lot more time at home rather than going out into the world. That, combined with the trauma of my sexual assault, has made me more or less unavailable for most forms of social interaction. With that in mind, there is something I feel I have to tell everyone.

Since the start of my recovery, I have felt incredibly distant from God. As I have said in earlier posts, my faith is a big part of who I am. Being away from it has made me feel as if I had lost one of my limbs. While I've always known it in my head that God is there, I have never felt less like it in my heart. It is the absence of such heartfelt feeling, that spiritual touch that I have been missing, that has left me feeling as if I were emotionally and spiritually paralyzed, unable to feel much of anything. I can understand, both intellectually and emotionally, that God is there, but I have felt a deep disconnect from the feeling of God that was normally present when I turned to spiritual matters.

I never understood as well as I do now when others have shared similar experiences. As a Christian, it's hard to say such a thing aloud. After all, wasn't Jesus supposed to provide that touch in my life? Wasn't His purpose to provide a connection directly to the heart of God? It has been difficult for me to admit that I have been missing out on one of the most important parts of my life, but I feel I must in order to share the good news.

You see, things have begun to turn around. I'm going to be honest, I don't know why. I am not going to speculate as to what might have caused it. Whatever the cause, it has led to a renewed sense of God's presence in my heart. That spiritual touch that I have been missing is back and I can't tell you how amazing it feels to have it back. It is as if a warm sun has finally come out after months of rain.

I just had to take the time to share that with you all because it has been such a big part of what life is all about for me. I'm sure you understand what I mean. For those of you who have been feeling the same thing, take heart. There is hope yet. I'm not sure how I regained the feeling, but regain it I have. I can only hope that it will return for you as well. The pain of the last nine months has been tempered, if not completely relieved, by the sense that I am no longer alone. Even if I were to fall to injury in this time when I am so unsteady on my feet, I wouldn't be alone. God is there to pick me up. He is there to help me heal. He is there to provide strength when mine is gone. He is my strength and my salvation. I know I have said that before, but it bears repeating. I know that I am never truly alone because God will always be with me. With such a knowledge in my heart, nothing can defeat me.

Suppose you have two children, one is a 10-year-old boy and the other is a 12-year-old girl. They tell you they wish to marry each other. You are very upset and feel that they are too young to make such an important decision, so you refuse to give your blessing. They say that they love each other very much and that they intend to run away together to get married. Is this child abuse?

—D.G., North Hollywood

I've never heard of any law that defines parental prevention of child marriage as child abuse. There's no way I could give an opinion as to whether that could or should be the law.

But I can tell you what I think. While I can understand both the children's position and the parents', the children don't--and legally can't--have the right to marry. Until then, the question of whether this is child abuse by the parents would depend on the parents' reasons for refusing to give their blessing.

For example, if the 10-year-old boy wants to get married only to have a younger wife, I would think it is not child abuse by the parents to prevent that. On the other hand, if the young are in love, and their reasons for wanting to marry are not unreasonable, I would think that the parents would be unfairly hurting their children if they prevented them from doing so. Then again, since neither child is old enough to enter into a marriage, the question of whether it was child abuse might be moot.

On the other hand, it might be that the parents should agree to the marriage on the condition that the young couple agree that they are not bound by this marriage if they change their minds once they reach the age of majority.

•••

If I am in a public place such as a department store and am robbed on the premises, is the store or the management of the store responsible for the loss?

—W.L.

It would appear that you are asking if a department store or other commercial business establishment is liable for your losses if you suffer a theft while in their premises. Since the establishment generally has "no control" over the criminal conduct of a thief, unless the business itself was negligent in some manner in preventing or controlling access to the stolen property, a business would probably not be liable under normal circumstances.

If a person is injured, and a close family member is the doctor, and for the sake of family peace, the doctor does not perform a necessary surgery, if the person dies as a result, is the doctor at risk of a law suit by the family member or the deceased's estate?

—O.C.S.

Yes. If a doctor has a patient who requires necessary medical treatment, and the doctor's reasons for not providing such treatment is only to avoid emotional family issues, then such behavior by the doctor would generally be totally inappropriate and inexcusable.

By choosing the path of refusing to treat a family member in order to avoid family issues, the doctor would be risking the health, well-being and indeed the very life of the family member. While a doctor cannot be held responsible for every failure of treatment, doctors certainly do not have the right to avoid performing medical procedures and endangering the very lives of a patient based simply on family issues.

In the event of a such a death, there probably would be a lawsuit based on medical malpractice, wrongful death, possibly battery and perhaps even elder abuse, depending on the circumstances.

What would you do if you couldn’t buy food from a store? Can you figure out 5 ways to make a fire without a match?

These are just some of the preparedness questions that we like to ask ourselves to ensure that our family can not only survive, but thrive without modern day conveniences. When you start thinking outside the box, you realize just how much stuff we have and how much we rely on that stuff to help us live our lives.

One of those items is a cooking stove. We are all so dependent on them and we tend to forget that there are other ways to cook your food without them. In times of crisis, fires might be a luxury that you can’t afford and you’ll quickly realize just how much you rely on them for your daily tasks. You must then think of other ways to cook all of that food without electricity, gas, or wood.

Here are 8 ways you can cook without a traditional kitchen or outside heat source.

## 1. How to Cook Without A Stove Using a Solar Oven

These are incredibly easy to make and will allow you to cook without any gas or electricity. If you can find a large box, an old piece of window, some cardboard, and tinfoil, you can create yourself a solar oven that can be used for all types of cooking and even dehydrating.

There are many videos and directions on the internet, but this is a very good DIY video tutorial on how make your own solar oven.

## 2. Cooking Without a stove with a Rocket Stove

A rocket stove is a very effective device that burns through a lot of fuel incredibly quickly, while remaining relatively safe because it uses a high-pressure, high-temperature combustion system that contains most of the heat and reduces the risk of fire.

It’s very efficient and lightweight which makes this a perfect option for outdoor cooking or even cooking during times of crisis. There are many plans and videos online, of how easy it is to make a Rocket Stove.

## 3. Cooking Without a Stove Using a Dutch Oven

Dutch ovens have been around for a long time and are used for cooking, braising, roasting, frying, and baking. It is a large pot with a tight-fitting lid that is ideal for all manner of cooking.

While many people use these on an open heating source, such as a campfire, you can also place a Dutch oven inside a pit made in a fire and allow it to cook all of your meals there, without a stove or electricity. They are incredibly versatile and will make your life much easier because of the amount of things you can cook inside.

## 4. Camping Stoves

We all know that camping stoves can be incredibly useful. The benefit of the fuel-run camping stoves is that they don’t require any electricity or wood and can easily be stored away for the times when you need it the most. They are highly portable and ideal for camping and hiking.

## 5. Outdoor Propane Burners

Propane burners are becoming increasingly popular for backyard cooking and barbecue parties as well as preppers who want to live off the land for extended periods of time. They are highly efficient, powerful, and very safe to use.

These are great if you are preparing for a bug out situation and want to make sure that you can cook your food quickly and efficiently.

## 6. Coleman Camping Stoves

Camping stoves can be incredibly useful. Coleman camping stoves can be fueled by small gas canisters and are highly portable, and are small enough to fit into backpacks, but powerful enough to cook many dishes within no time at all.

Their range of camping stoves includes dual fuel camping stoves, butane camping stoves, propane camping stove, and even liquid fuel stoves.

## 7. How to Cook Without a Stove Using a Steam Box

This is for those who not only like to cook, but also like to recycle. If you find yourself without a stove, you can make a steam box with items you recycle. This can be made from old milk or paint carton, an old aluminum can or a piece of PVC pipe. It makes use of steam, which is an environmentally friendly way to cook.

## 8. Sterno Stoves

Sterno stoves or canned heat are a very efficient and easy way to cook your food without a stove. They are a great option for camping or prepping since you can use them for boiling water and preparing hot meals.

The little fuel canisters are incredibly cheap (from $1 -to $3) and will burn for a long time.

These are just a few ways we can all learn to cook without a traditional stove. Our dependency on electricity is becoming greater and greater and that is why it’s important to explore different options such as the ones above.

Do you have any tips or ideas on cooking without a stove? Tell us in the comments and let’s get the word out in case of any emergencies!

Question: If all beds disappeared, where would you sleep?
Answer:  What would you do if you couldn’t buy food from a store? Can you figure out 5 ways to make a fire without a match?

These are just some of the preparedness questions that we like to ask ourselves to ensure that our family can not only survive, but thrive without modern day conveniences. When you start thinking outside the box, you realize just how much stuff we have and how much we rely on that stuff to help us live our lives.

One of those items is a cooking stove. We are all so dependent on them and we tend to forget that there are other ways to cook your food without them. In times of crisis, fires might be a luxury that you can’t afford and you’ll quickly realize just how much you rely on them for your daily tasks. You must then think of other ways to cook all of that food without electricity, gas, or wood.

Here are 8 ways you can cook without a traditional kitchen or outside heat source.

## 1. How to Cook Without A Stove Using a Solar Oven

These are incredibly easy to make and will allow you to cook without any gas or electricity. If you can find a large box, an old piece of window, some cardboard, and tinfoil, you can create yourself a solar oven that can be used for all types of cooking and even dehydrating.

There are many videos and directions on the internet, but this is a very good DIY video tutorial on how make your own solar oven.

## 2. Cooking Without a stove with a Rocket Stove

A rocket stove is a very effective device that burns through a lot of fuel incredibly quickly, while remaining relatively safe because it uses a high-pressure, high-temperature combustion system that contains most of the heat and reduces the risk of fire.

It’s very efficient and lightweight which makes this a perfect option for outdoor cooking or even cooking during times of crisis. There are many plans and videos online, of how easy it is to make a Rocket Stove.

## 3. Cooking Without a Stove Using a Dutch Oven

Dutch ovens have been around for a long time and are used for cooking, braising, roasting, frying, and baking. It is a large pot with a tight-fitting lid that is ideal for all manner of cooking.

While many people use these on an open heating source, such as a campfire, you can also place a Dutch oven inside a pit made in a fire and allow it to cook all of your meals there, without a stove or electricity. They are incredibly versatile and will make your life much easier because of the amount of things you can cook inside.

## 4. Camping Stoves

We all know that camping stoves can be incredibly useful. The benefit of the fuel-run camping stoves is that they don’t require any electricity or wood and can easily be stored away for the times when you need it the most. They are highly portable and ideal for camping and hiking.

## 5. Outdoor Propane Burners

Propane burners are becoming increasingly popular for backyard cooking and barbecue parties as well as preppers who want to live off the land for extended periods of time. They are highly efficient, powerful, and very safe to use.

These are great if you are preparing for a bug out situation and want to make sure that you can cook your food quickly and efficiently.

## 6. Coleman Camping Stoves

Camping stoves can be incredibly useful. Coleman camping stoves can be fueled by small gas canisters and are highly portable, and are small enough to fit into backpacks, but powerful enough to cook many dishes within no time at all.

Their range of camping stoves includes dual fuel camping stoves, butane camping stoves, propane camping stove, and even liquid fuel stoves.

## 7. How to Cook Without a Stove Using a Steam Box

This is for those who not only like to cook, but also like to recycle. If you find yourself without a stove, you can make a steam box with items you recycle. This can be made from old milk or paint carton, an old aluminum can or a piece of PVC pipe. It makes use of steam, which is an environmentally friendly way to cook.

## 8. Sterno Stoves

Sterno stoves or canned heat are a very efficient and easy way to cook your food without a stove. They are a great option for camping or prepping since you can use them for boiling water and preparing hot meals.

The little fuel canisters are incredibly cheap (from $1 -to $3) and will burn for a long time.

These are just a few ways we can all learn to cook without a traditional stove. Our dependency on electricity is becoming greater and greater and that is why it’s important to explore different options such as the ones above.

Do you have any tips or ideas on cooking without a stove? Tell us in the comments and let’s get the word out in case of any emergencies!

AR glasses can be programmed to synchronize with others so that multiple users share the same experience simultaneously, providing a social aspect.
3. Home installation of inflatable movie screens: Portable, inflatable screens can be set up in people's backyards or living rooms. Rentals would be available for people who want periodic cinema experiences without owning the equipment. Additionally, friends and neighbours could club together to have a communal experience at one person's house.
4. Car cinema projections: Develop a projection technology that links into the car's GPS system so that movies can be projected onto the road or the surroundings. Passengers in the vehicles can watch films during travel, synchronising playback across multiple cars for road trips.
5. Immersive sound pods: Develop private pods equipped with audio systems capable of providing 3D audio. The pods would be placed in public spaces like parks, creating a unique experience where users can feel immersed in the soundscape of a movie, even without visuals.

9. Interactive movie sets: Allow users to participate in an interactive film set as characters, interacting with their physical environment and each other to create a unique, choose-your-own-adventure style experience.
10. Intimate cinema experiences: Create miniature, personal cinemas catering to one or two people. Designed for private movie screenings, these intimate theatres would provide an upscale, exclusive experience for couples or solo movie enthusiasts.
11. Dinner and a movie experience: Introduce dine-in restaurants featuring movie projections, where customers can enjoy a themed meal for each film while watching. Menu designs would include food, décor and ambience based on the story.

13. Motion capture live stage performances: Create live performances where actors use motion capture technology to re-enact iconic movies in real-time, adding new dimensions and scenes for a more interactive theatre experience.

For a start we need a visual component, we need something for our audience to watch. So we will be needing some sort of projector or monitor that can do the job of displaying our content.

Since we do not have studio produced films to watch anymore, how do we create a film like experience without studios?

First of all, we could start writing screenplays, that is writing a script for our story. It will need to contain the story, the characters, dialogs, and stage directions, etc. Writing a screenplay is not an easy task and if you are not used to it, you will have to practice to get the hang of it.

Then, once this is done, we need to cast people in our story. We will need to select who plays which role and make sure they are believable for the position.

Since we can no longer hire a professional camera crew or use studios rigs, we will need to build our own setup. This means we will need to buy, borrow, or rent the equipment we need to shoot our movie.

Then we will need actual locations where we can shoot our movie. Since we are not in a studio, we will be needing to find the places where we can stage each scene. If you are set on doing this and do not have access to a house, a garage, a wood, any open area, etc you may have to build it yourself.

Once the shooting is over, we will need to edit our footage using editing software that exist for this purpose. This will take additional time and effort but once you know what you are doing, it is not a difficult task.

Now we have all the material to create our cinematic experience, it is just a matter of making sure that the audience enjoys it!

For people who have trouble getting to sleep at night, a great solution is to use a weighted body pillow. While traditional sleep pillows are often stuffed with lightweight materials, weighted pillows are usually filled with grains, sand, plastic pellets, or beads instead. With all these heavy materials pushing down on your head and neck, it can help to relieve tension, stress, and anxiety during sleep.

While there has been some research conducted on the use of weighted blankets and therapeutic pillows, the studies are limited, so it can be difficult to determine just how effective weighted body pillows can be for improving sleep. With that being said, many people who have used a weighted body pillow say that it has helped them fall asleep faster, stay asleep longer, and feel more rested when they wake up in the morning. If you're curious about what these special pillows have to offer, here's what to look for when shopping for one.

## What to Look for in a Weighted Body Pillow

### Weight

Weighted body pillows can come in various weights, and it is important to find one that feels right for you. If the pillow is too heavy, then you may feel uncomfortable during use. Conversely, if the pillow is too light, it may not provide the benefits you need. Most weighted pillows use removable bead inserts, so you can take weights out or add more as necessary to adjust the feel of the pillow.

As a general rule, aim for a body pillow that is approximately ten percent of your total body weight. This amount may vary slightly depending on your personal preferences and your physical needs. For example, if you are an average-sized adult and you are using the pillow to alleviate restless leg syndrome, then a lighter pillow might be more appropriate. On the other hand, if you are much larger, or if you are trying to treat post-traumatic stress disorder or another mental health condition, a heavier pillow might be more appropriate for your needs.

### Filling

Weighted pillows can be filled in various ways, but most use small polypropylene (PP) pellets. PP is a synthetic plastic, and it is lightweight, odorless, and non-absorbent. As such, these pellets will not harbor bacteria, mold, or mildew. They also will not compress over time, so the pillow should maintain its shape and provide support for years to come.

Weighted body pillows can also be filled with rice, buckwheat, or sand. However, these substances can go rancid, and they can also attract pests. Plus, they can become deformed over time, so the pillow may not last as long as one filled with PP pellets.

### Cover

The outer cover of the pillow should be soft, breathable, and machine-washable. There are a variety of materials you can choose from, including cotton, linen, silk, and other natural and synthetic fabrics. But cotton, the most common filling for these pillows, is also the most breathable. And since airflow is so important for getting a good night's sleep, we recommend selecting a pillow with a cotton cover.

Additionally, look for one with a zippered cover. A zipper will allow you to easily remove the cover for washing, and it will also ensure that the filling stays securely inside.

### Size

Weighted body pillows vary in size, and it is a good idea to measure the space in your bed or your sleeping area before purchasing one. The pillow should be large enough to wrap around your entire body, but it shouldn't be so big that it takes up all of your bed space.

Most weighted body pillows are approximately 5 feet long, which should be enough to support your neck and shoulders when you sleep on your side. If you are much taller than average, then you may want to consider purchasing a larger weighted body pillow.

### Cleaning Instructions

Caring for your weighted pillow correctly is an important part of ensuring its longevity. First, invest in a pillow protector or a waterproof pillow cover to use as the first line of defense against stains, dust mites, and allergens. Then, read the cleaning instructions before doing anything else. Many pillows are machine washable, but you should always use the gentle cycle and a gentle detergent. Also, wash and dry the cover separately, as it will typically need to be cleaned more frequently than the inner pillowcase.

The inner pillowcase can generally be spot-cleaned, or you can use a mild detergent to hand wash it in the sink. Be careful to not squeeze or wring the pillow, as this can damage the filling. Instead, you should allow it to air dry over a fan or other ventilated area.

## How to Use a Weighted Body Pillow

It's not enough to simply place a weighted body pillow on your bed. It must be properly positioned for it to work as intended.

The first step to using a weighted body pillow for sleep is to place it behind your back while you are lying down. With your shoulders, arms, hips, knees, and ankles in proper alignment, wrap your arms around the pillow and pull it up against your chest. Then, rest your head on the pillow and allow your shoulders to relax. Your neck should be in a neutral position where there is minimal strain.

If you have trouble staying asleep at night, try placing the pillow between your legs to keep your knees aligned. The pressure from the pillow can help to distribute your weight evenly, thereby reducing the chances of you waking up throughout the night due to hip or leg pain.

Keep in mind that it will probably take a little bit of time to get used to the weighted body pillow. Don't be discouraged if you have trouble sleeping with it at first. Over time, your body should adjust to the extra weight, and you may find that you are sleeping more deeply and comfortably than ever before.

Weighted body pillows can be extremely beneficial for people who struggle to fall asleep and stay asleep at night. However, it is important to purchase a high-quality weighted body pillow and to use it correctly for maximum benefit. The right weight, filling, cover, size, and cleaning instructions can ensure the long-term health of your new sleep accessory, and proper use can help you get a better night's sleep on a consistent basis.

output.text_cot:
First, you would have to find a material that could replace gold or silver, then you would need to produce a material which could be a credible replacement for gem stones and at the end, it would be necessary to create a design which would match these new materials' properties. But let's say that the situation changes and gold and precious stones don't disappear, but instead get more expensive, and it's no longer desirable to use them. This time you have to act fast, as everyone else is probably already looking for alternatives. What would you do?

The above scenario was actually the situation that existed at the end of the 19th century. During this time, gold and all precious metals became so expensive, due to the gold rush in the western USA, that it no longer became profitable to use precious metals in ornamental design. Instead of jewels, manufacturers started to use glass and crystals imitating precious stones. There was one problem though: what do you use as an alternative for precious metals?

At that time, the British Empire, with its centre in London, was the most powerful state in the world. London played the role a kind of world centre for trade and craftsmanship. The leading countries in terms of new craftsmanship solutions were mainly countries connected with the British Empire. It was in Europe, particularly in France and Germany, where new material solutions were sought.

Although there were many new solutions in production, the one which succeeded the most was a material called "German Silver", or today: Nickel silver (Ni Ag Cu). Nickel silver is a metal alloy, mainly composed of copper, nickel and zinc, but also sometimes with small amounts of tin and lead. It is called German silver because in the mid-19th century, most of the production of nickel silver was in Germany. When compared with gold, the main advantage of nickel silver is that it does not corrode, making it ideal for use in ornament manufacture.

This material, together with the production techniques used, changed the direction of ornament production, in which the traditional technique of lost wax casting was replaced with a new one called die casting. This method involves injecting the molten nickel silver at high speed within a steel mould through a gooseneck (hence the name gooseneck casting). The mould is made so that the material can penetrate into the smallest details, creating the surface decoration of the ornament directly from the mould.

One of the main advantages of this technique is that the mould can remain unchanged, or can be used many times, in some cases even hundreds of times. The ornaments produced in this way are lighter but more durable, and the production itself can be up to several thousands of times cheaper than before.

Because this material is much cheaper than precious metals, even when combined with precious stones, it is still impossible to create a value equivalent to objects made of precious metals with precious stones set in them. But for those products to be desirable, their price must be significantly reduced and mass production made possible. The cheapness of the method in itself is, however, not enough to change the perception of the value of an object. The value of mass-produced ornaments must be increased by adding the perception of uniqueness, for example hand-painted decoration or enamel.

But how is it possible to make hundreds of the same items appear unique?

The technique which was used the most is still used today - enamelling (enamel application). The most common method of using enamel techniques is Champlevé (the technique in which recesses are created on the surface of a metal object and filled in with enamel ). This technique creates an effect where the surface is divided, usually according to a grid structure, which remains in the background. This background was usually filled in with a transparent enamel to achieve a clear division of the surface and a high contrast which can highlight the hand painted parts.

The most common shapes of enamelled products created using the gooseneck cast method were plates, boxes, caskets, picture frames and all kinds of jewellery. The themes of the motifs were most often in the form of flowers (mainly roses) and decorative patterns similar to art nouveau style motifs. This was because the nickel silver and enamel are very similar in hue and it is very difficult to achieve a contrast between these materials and paint motifs with a different colour. Even today, you can see that the most used colour is white and blue or opaque enamel in different nuances, while other bright and intensive colours are rarely used.

The most common production technique used was not limited to ornaments made from nickel silver, or enamel work, but was also used for all other ornaments made from other cheaper materials, such as: cast iron, brass, tin and even wood. This technique made mass-produced objects available to people who in the past could not afford them. It had the greatest impact before the Second World War; however, after the war, the nickel silver technique started to fade.

Enamel work, just like techniques of die casting, is still popular today and is used in all kinds of objects, from fine art, to industrial or automotive design.

Enamel design was not the only mass-production technique of this period. In the following articles, we will write of the development of mass production of glass and ceramics in the art nouveau style.

Martin Jan Straka is a designer and a creator of jewellery brand LUZIA.

For the first time, he dealt with crafts and design in his childhood, when he created the first pieces of clothing, toys and pieces of furniture for his sister's dolls. For a short time, he abandoned his creativity for business and finance studies. After completing his studies, he worked in finance for five years.
